1.0.oldText: Few features of our current knowledge are more surprising, or more telling of how little progress we have made in thinking about the most important subjects, than the lack of resolution in the long debate over the criterion of right and wrong. From the beginning of philosophy, the question of the highest good — which is the same as asking what morality is grounded in — has been treated as the central problem of speculative thought. It has occupied the most gifted minds and divided them into rival schools waging fierce intellectual war against one another. After more than two thousand years, the same disputes go on. Philosophers still line up under the same opposing banners, and neither professional thinkers nor humanity at large seem any closer to agreement than they were when the young Socrates listened to old Protagoras and defended (if Plato's dialogue is based on a real conversation) the theory of utilitarianism against the popular morality of the so-called sophist.

1.1.oldText: It is true that similar confusion and uncertainty — sometimes outright disagreement — exists about the first principles of every science, including the one widely regarded as the most certain: mathematics. Yet this rarely damages, and usually does not damage at all, the trustworthiness of the conclusions those sciences reach. The apparent paradox is explained by the fact that the detailed doctrines of a science are not usually derived from, or supported by, what we call its first principles. If they were, no science would be on shakier ground than algebra, whose certainty does not come from the elementary axioms typically taught to beginners — axioms which, as some of its most eminent teachers have framed them, are as full of fictions as English law and as full of mysteries as theology. The truths eventually accepted as a science's first principles are really the final results of metaphysical analysis applied to the basic notions that science works with. Their relation to the science is not that of foundations to a building, but of roots to a tree, which can do their job perfectly well even if they are never dug up and exposed to view. But while in the sciences particular truths come before the general theory, one might expect the opposite to be true of a practical art like morals or legislation. Every action is taken for the sake of some end, and rules of action would seem to take their entire character and tone from the end they serve. When we engage in any pursuit, a clear and precise conception of what we are pursuing would seem to be the first thing we need, not the last thing we are working toward. A test of right and wrong, one would think, must be the means of figuring out what is right or wrong, not a consequence of having already figured it out.

1.2.oldText: This difficulty cannot be sidestepped by appealing to the popular theory of a natural faculty — a moral sense or instinct that tells us what is right and what is wrong. For one thing, the very existence of such a moral instinct is itself part of the dispute. And those believers in it who have any claim to philosophical seriousness have been forced to give up the idea that it identifies what is right or wrong in any particular case the way our other senses identify a sight or a sound right in front of us. Our moral faculty, according to all of its interpreters who deserve to be called thinkers, supplies us only with the general principles of moral judgment. It is a branch of reason, not of perception, and we must look to it for the abstract doctrines of morality, not for direct perception of morality in concrete cases. The intuitive school of ethics, just as much as what might be called the inductive school, insists on the necessity of general laws. Both agree that whether an individual action is moral is not a question of direct perception, but of applying a law to a particular case. They also largely recognise the same moral laws — but they differ on the evidence for those laws and the source of their authority. According to one view, the principles of morals are self-evident a priori, requiring nothing more than that the meaning of the terms be understood. According to the other, right and wrong, like truth and falsehood, are questions of observation and experience. But both hold equally that morality must be derived from principles, and the intuitive school affirms just as strongly as the inductive school that there is such a thing as a science of morals. Yet they rarely try to spell out the list of a priori principles that are supposed to serve as the premises of this science, and they make even less effort to reduce those various principles to one first principle or common ground of obligation. They either assume the ordinary precepts of morality have a priori authority, or they offer as the common foundation of those maxims some generality far less obviously authoritative than the maxims themselves — a generality that has never gained popular acceptance. Yet if their claims are to hold up, there ought to be either one fundamental principle or law at the root of all morality, or, if there are several, a definite order of precedence among them. And the one principle, or the rule for deciding between principles when they conflict, ought to be self-evident.

1.3.oldText: To ask how far the bad effects of this gap have been softened in practice, or how badly the moral beliefs of humanity have been corrupted or made uncertain by the absence of any clear ultimate standard, would require a complete survey and critique of past and present ethical doctrine. But it is easy to show that whatever steadiness or consistency those moral beliefs have achieved is mainly due to the unacknowledged influence of a standard people will not admit they are using. Although the lack of an openly recognised first principle has made ethics less a guide and more a rubber stamp for what people already feel, still — since people's feelings, both of approval and disapproval, are heavily shaped by what they take to be the effects of things on their happiness — the principle of utility, or as Bentham later called it, the greatest-happiness principle, has had a large hand in shaping the moral doctrines even of those who most scornfully reject its authority. Nor is there any school of thought that refuses to admit that the effect of actions on happiness is a deeply important, even dominant, consideration in many of the practical details of morality — however reluctant such schools are to recognise it as the fundamental principle of morality and the source of moral obligation. I could go further and say that for all a priori moralists who think they need to argue at all, utilitarian arguments are indispensable. It is not my present purpose to criticise these thinkers, but I cannot help pointing, for illustration, to a systematic treatise by one of the most illustrious of them: the Metaphysics of Ethics by Kant. This remarkable man, whose system of thought will long remain one of the landmarks in the history of philosophy, does in that work lay down a universal first principle as the source and ground of moral obligation. It runs: 'Act so that the rule on which you act could be adopted as a law by all rational beings.' But when he sets out to derive from this maxim any of the actual duties of morality, he fails — almost ridiculously — to show that there would be any contradiction, any logical (let alone physical) impossibility, in all rational beings adopting the most outrageously immoral rules of conduct. All he actually shows is that the consequences of universal adoption would be such as no one would want to bring on themselves.

1.4.oldText: In this essay, without further discussion of rival theories, I will try to contribute something to the understanding and appreciation of the Utilitarian or Happiness theory, and to give it whatever proof it is capable of receiving. Clearly this cannot be proof in the ordinary and popular sense of the word. Questions of ultimate ends are not open to direct proof. Whatever can be proved to be good must be shown to be so by being shown to be a means to something already admitted to be good without proof. The medical art is proved to be good because it leads to health — but how can it be proved that health is good? The art of music is good, among other reasons, because it produces pleasure — but what proof can be given that pleasure is good? If, then, it is claimed that there is a comprehensive formula that includes all things which are in themselves good, and that whatever else is good is good not as an end but as a means, the formula may be accepted or rejected, but it is not the subject of what is commonly understood as proof. We are not, however, to conclude that whether to accept or reject it must depend on blind impulse or arbitrary choice. There is a wider meaning of the word proof in which this question is as open to it as any other disputed question in philosophy. The subject falls within the scope of the rational faculty, and reason does not handle it only by intuition. Considerations can be presented which are capable of inclining the intellect either to grant or to withhold its assent — and that is equivalent to proof.

1.5.oldText: We will soon examine what kinds of considerations these are, how they apply to the case, and what rational grounds can be given for accepting or rejecting the utilitarian formula. But a preliminary condition for rational acceptance or rejection is that the formula be correctly understood. I believe the very imperfect notion ordinarily formed of its meaning is the main obstacle to its reception, and that if it could be cleared of even the cruder misunderstandings, the question would be greatly simplified and a large share of its difficulties removed. Before turning, then, to the philosophical grounds for endorsing the utilitarian standard, I will offer some clarifications of the doctrine itself, in order to make clearer what it is, to distinguish it from what it is not, and to dispose of those practical objections to it which either arise from, or are closely connected with, mistaken interpretations of its meaning. Having thus prepared the ground, I will afterwards try to throw what light I can on the question, considered as one of philosophical theory.

2.0.oldText: Only a passing remark is needed for the ignorant blunder of supposing that those who defend utility as the test of right and wrong use the term in the narrow, colloquial sense in which utility is opposed to pleasure. An apology is owed to the philosophical opponents of utilitarianism for even momentarily appearing to confuse them with anyone capable of so absurd a misunderstanding. It is the more remarkable because the opposite charge — that utilitarianism reduces everything to pleasure, and that in its grossest form — is another of the common accusations against it. As an able writer has pointedly remarked, the same kind of people, often the very same people, denounce the theory "as impracticably dry when the word utility precedes the word pleasure, and as too practicably voluptuous when the word pleasure precedes the word utility." Anyone who knows anything about the matter is aware that every writer from Epicurus to Bentham who upheld the theory of utility meant by it not something to be set against pleasure, but pleasure itself, together with freedom from pain. Far from setting the useful against the agreeable or the ornamental, they have always insisted that the useful means these, among other things. Yet the common herd, including the herd of writers — in newspapers and periodicals as well as in books of weight and pretension — keep falling into this shallow mistake. Having picked up the word utilitarian, knowing nothing about it but its sound, they habitually use it to denote the rejection or neglect of pleasure in some of its forms: of beauty, of ornament, or of amusement. The term is misapplied in this ignorant way not only as criticism, but occasionally as a compliment, as though it implied superiority to frivolity and the mere pleasures of the moment. This perverted usage is the only one in which the word is popularly known, and the only source from which the next generation is getting its sense of what it means. Those who introduced the word, but who long ago stopped using it as a label of their own, may well feel called upon to take it up again if by doing so they can hope to rescue it from this complete degradation.[A]

2.1.oldText: The creed that takes Utility, or the Greatest Happiness Principle, as the foundation of morality holds that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness, and wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness. By happiness it means pleasure and the absence of pain; by unhappiness, pain and the loss of pleasure. To give a clear picture of the moral standard set up by the theory, much more needs to be said — in particular, what the theory includes under the ideas of pain and pleasure, and to what extent it leaves that an open question. But these further explanations do not affect the theory of life on which this theory of morality rests: namely, that pleasure and freedom from pain are the only things desirable as ends, and that all desirable things (which are as numerous in the utilitarian scheme as in any other) are desirable either for the pleasure inherent in themselves or as means of promoting pleasure and preventing pain.

2.2.oldText: Now this theory of life provokes deep dislike in many minds, including some of the most admirable in feeling and purpose. The idea that life has, as they put it, no higher end than pleasure — no better and nobler object of desire and pursuit — they call utterly mean and grovelling, a doctrine fit only for swine. The followers of Epicurus were compared to swine from very early on, and modern holders of the doctrine are occasionally treated to equally polite comparisons by its German, French, and English critics.

2.3.oldText: When attacked this way, the Epicureans have always answered that it is not they, but their accusers, who portray human nature in a degrading light. The charge presupposes that human beings are capable of no pleasures except those swine are capable of. If that were true, the accusation could not be denied — but it would no longer be a reproach. For if the sources of pleasure were exactly the same for humans and for swine, the rule of life good enough for one would be good enough for the other. The comparison of the Epicurean life to that of beasts feels degrading precisely because a beast's pleasures do not satisfy a human being's conception of happiness. Human beings have faculties more elevated than the animal appetites, and once they become conscious of those faculties they do not regard anything as happiness which does not include their gratification. I do not consider the Epicureans to have been at all faultless in working out their account of which consequences follow from the utilitarian principle. To do that adequately, many Stoic and Christian elements would need to be included. But there is no known Epicurean theory of life which does not assign to the pleasures of the intellect, the feelings and imagination, and the moral sentiments a much higher value as pleasures than to those of mere sensation. It must be admitted, however, that utilitarian writers in general have located the superiority of mental over bodily pleasures mainly in the greater permanence, safety, low cost, and so on, of the former — that is, in their circumstantial advantages rather than in their intrinsic nature. On all those points utilitarians have fully made their case, but they might have taken the other, higher ground with complete consistency. It is entirely compatible with the principle of utility to recognise that some kinds of pleasure are more desirable and more valuable than others. It would be absurd to suppose that, while in valuing every other thing we consider both quality and quantity, the valuing of pleasures should depend on quantity alone.

2.4.oldText: If I am asked what I mean by a difference of quality in pleasures, or what makes one pleasure more valuable than another simply as a pleasure, apart from being greater in amount, there is only one possible answer. Of two pleasures, if there is one which all or almost all who have experience of both decidedly prefer, with no feeling of moral obligation to prefer it, that is the more desirable pleasure. If one of the two is, by those competently acquainted with both, placed so far above the other that they prefer it even knowing it brings a greater amount of discontent with it, and would not give it up for any quantity of the other pleasure their nature is capable of, we are justified in saying that the preferred enjoyment has a superiority in quality so great that it makes quantity, by comparison, count for little.

2.5.oldText: Now it is an unquestionable fact that those equally acquainted with both and equally capable of appreciating and enjoying both give a marked preference to the mode of existence that exercises their higher faculties. Few human beings would agree to be turned into a lower animal in return for a promise of the fullest allowance of a beast's pleasures. No intelligent human being would consent to be a fool, no educated person would be an ignoramus, no person of feeling and conscience would be selfish and base, even if they were convinced that the fool, the dunce, or the rascal is more satisfied with his lot than they are with theirs. They would not give up what they have over and above him for the most complete satisfaction of all the desires they share with him. If they ever imagine they would, it is only in cases of suffering so extreme that to escape it they would trade their lot for almost anyone else's, however undesirable in their own eyes. A being with higher faculties needs more to make him happy, is probably capable of more acute suffering, and is certainly vulnerable to it at more points, than a being of an inferior type — but despite these liabilities, he can never really wish to sink into what he feels to be a lower grade of existence. We can explain this unwillingness however we like: we may attribute it to pride, a word indiscriminately used for some of the most and some of the least admirable feelings humans are capable of; we may trace it to the love of liberty and personal independence, the appeal to which was one of the Stoics' most effective tools for inculcating it; or to the love of power, or the love of excitement, both of which do really enter into and feed it. But its most appropriate name is a sense of dignity, which all human beings have in one form or another, in some rough but not exact proportion to their higher faculties, and which is so essential a part of the happiness of those in whom it is strong that nothing in conflict with it can be more than momentarily an object of desire for them. Anyone who supposes that this preference involves sacrificing happiness — that the superior being, under anything like equal circumstances, is not happier than the inferior one — is confusing the very different ideas of happiness and contentment. There is no question that the being whose capacities for enjoyment are low has the best chance of getting them fully satisfied, and that a highly endowed being will always feel that any happiness available to him, given the way the world is, is imperfect. But he can learn to bear its imperfections, if they are at all bearable, and they will not make him envy the being who is unconscious of those imperfections — but only because he does not feel the good which those imperfections qualify. It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. And if the fool, or the pig, is of a different opinion, it is because they only know their own side of the question. The other party to the comparison knows both sides.

2.6.oldText: It may be objected that many who are capable of the higher pleasures occasionally, under temptation, postpone them in favour of the lower. But this is fully compatible with a complete appreciation of the intrinsic superiority of the higher. People often, out of weakness of character, choose the nearer good even when they know it is the less valuable — and this happens just as much when the choice is between two bodily pleasures as when it is between bodily and mental pleasure. They pursue sensual indulgences to the damage of their health, while perfectly aware that health is the greater good. It may be further objected that many who start out with youthful enthusiasm for everything noble sink, as they age, into indolence and selfishness. But I do not believe that those who undergo this very common change voluntarily choose the lower kind of pleasures over the higher. I believe that before they devote themselves exclusively to one, they have already become incapable of the other. The capacity for nobler feelings is in most natures a very tender plant, easily killed not only by hostile influences but by simple want of nourishment. In the majority of young people it quickly dies away if the occupations imposed on them by their position in life, and the society they have been thrown into, are not conducive to keeping that higher capacity in exercise. People lose their high aspirations as they lose their intellectual tastes, because they have neither the time nor the opportunity to indulge them, and they become addicted to inferior pleasures not because they deliberately prefer them, but because those are either the only ones available to them, or the only ones they are any longer capable of enjoying. It is doubtful whether anyone who has remained equally susceptible to both classes of pleasures has ever knowingly and calmly preferred the lower — though many, in every age, have broken down in a futile attempt to combine both.

2.7.oldText: From this verdict of the only competent judges, I think there can be no appeal. On the question of which of two pleasures is more worth having, or which of two ways of life is more gratifying to the feelings — apart from its moral attributes and consequences — the judgment of those qualified by knowledge of both, or, if they disagree, of the majority among them, must be accepted as final. There is even less reason to hesitate in accepting this judgment about the quality of pleasures, because there is no other tribunal to appeal to even on the question of quantity. What means do we have for determining which of two pains is sharper, or which of two pleasant sensations is more intense, except the general consensus of those familiar with both? Pains are not homogeneous, pleasures are not homogeneous, and pain and pleasure are always heterogeneous with each other. What can decide whether a particular pleasure is worth purchasing at the cost of a particular pain, except the feelings and judgment of those who have experienced them? When, therefore, those feelings and judgments declare the pleasures derived from the higher faculties to be preferable in kind, apart from any question of intensity, to those which the animal nature, cut off from the higher faculties, can feel, they are entitled to the same authority on this point.

2.8.oldText: I have dwelt on this point because it is a necessary part of a fully just conception of Utility or Happiness considered as the guiding rule of human conduct. But it is by no means an indispensable condition for accepting the utilitarian standard, because that standard is not the agent's own greatest happiness, but the greatest amount of happiness altogether. Even if it might be doubted whether a noble character is always happier for its nobleness, there can be no doubt that it makes other people happier and that the world in general is enormously better off because of it. Utilitarianism could therefore only achieve its end through the general cultivation of nobility of character, even if each individual were only benefited by the nobility of others, and his own nobility, so far as his happiness is concerned, were a sheer loss. But merely stating such an absurdity makes a refutation unnecessary.

2.9.oldText: According to the Greatest Happiness Principle, as explained above, the ultimate end — that with reference to and for the sake of which all other things are desirable, whether we are considering our own good or other people's — is an existence as free as possible from pain, and as rich as possible in enjoyments, both in quantity and quality. The test of quality, and the rule for measuring it against quantity, is the preference felt by those who, given their range of experience and their habits of self-consciousness and self-observation, are best equipped to compare. This, in the utilitarian view, is the end of human action, and so it is necessarily also the standard of morality. Morality can thus be defined as the rules and precepts for human conduct by following which an existence such as has been described might be secured, as far as possible, to all humankind — and not only to them, but, as far as the nature of things admits, to the whole world of sentient beings.

2.10.oldText: Against this doctrine, however, arises another class of objector who says that happiness, in any form, cannot be the rational purpose of human life and action — first, because it is unattainable. They contemptuously ask: What right have you to be happy? — a question Mr. Carlyle clinches by adding: What right, a short time ago, had you even to exist? Next, they say, human beings can do without happiness; that all noble human beings have felt this, and could not have become noble except by learning the lesson of Entsagen, or renunciation — a lesson which, thoroughly learnt and accepted, they assert is the beginning and necessary condition of all virtue.

2.11.oldText: The first of these objections would strike at the root of the matter if it were well founded; for if no happiness is to be had at all by human beings, the attainment of it cannot be the end of morality or of any rational conduct. Even in that case, however, something could still be said for the utilitarian theory, since utility includes not only the pursuit of happiness but the prevention or relief of unhappiness — and if the former aim is illusory, there is all the more scope and more urgent need for the latter, at least as long as human beings think it worth living and do not take refuge in the mass suicide recommended under certain conditions by Novalis. When it is positively asserted that it is impossible for human life to be happy, however, the claim, if not just a verbal quibble, is at least an exaggeration. If by happiness is meant a continuous run of intensely pleasurable excitement, then clearly that is impossible. A state of exalted pleasure lasts only moments, or, in some cases and with intermissions, hours or days; it is the occasional brilliant flash of enjoyment, not its permanent and steady flame. The philosophers who taught that happiness is the end of life were as fully aware of this as those who mock them. The happiness they meant was not a life of rapture, but moments of such rapture in an existence made up of few and transitory pains, many and varied pleasures, with a decided predominance of the active over the passive, and with this at the foundation of the whole: not to expect more from life than it is capable of giving. A life so composed has always seemed worthy of the name of happiness to those lucky enough to obtain it. And such an existence is even now the lot of many people for a considerable portion of their lives. The present wretched education and wretched social arrangements are the only real obstacle to its being attainable by almost everyone.

2.12.oldText: The objectors may perhaps doubt whether human beings, if taught to regard happiness as the end of life, would be satisfied with such a modest share of it. But great numbers of mankind have been satisfied with much less. The main components of a satisfied life appear to be two, either of which on its own is often enough for the purpose: tranquillity, and excitement. With plenty of tranquillity, many find they can be content with very little pleasure; with plenty of excitement, many can reconcile themselves to a considerable amount of pain. There is certainly no inherent impossibility in enabling even the bulk of mankind to unite both — since the two, far from being incompatible, are in natural alliance, with the prolongation of either being a preparation for, and stimulating a desire for, the other. It is only those whose indolence amounts to a vice who do not want excitement after a period of rest; it is only those whose need for excitement is a kind of disease who feel the tranquillity that follows excitement to be dull and insipid, instead of pleasurable in direct proportion to the excitement that came before it. When people who are reasonably well off in their outward circumstances do not find enough enjoyment in life to make it worthwhile, the cause is generally that they care for nobody but themselves. To those who have neither public nor private affections, the excitements of life are much reduced, and in any case lose value as the time approaches when all selfish interests must be ended by death. Those who leave behind them objects of personal affection, and especially those who have also cultivated a fellow feeling with the collective interests of mankind, keep a lively interest in life on the eve of death just as in the prime of youth and health. Next to selfishness, the principal cause of life being unsatisfactory is lack of mental cultivation. A cultivated mind — I do not mean that of a philosopher, but any mind to which the sources of knowledge have been opened, and which has been taught to a reasonable degree to use its faculties — finds sources of inexhaustible interest in everything around it: in the objects of nature, the achievements of art, the imaginations of poetry, the events of history, the ways of mankind past and present, and their prospects in the future. It is possible, indeed, to become indifferent to all this without having explored a thousandth part of it — but only if one has from the beginning had no moral or human interest in these things and has looked to them only for the gratification of curiosity.

2.13.oldText: There is absolutely no reason in the nature of things why a level of mental culture sufficient to give an intelligent interest in these objects of contemplation should not be the inheritance of everyone born in a civilised country. Just as little is there any inherent necessity that any human being should be a selfish egoist, with no feeling or care beyond those centred on his own miserable individuality. Something far better than that is already common enough now to give ample proof of what the human species might be made into. Genuine private affections and a sincere interest in the public good are possible, though in unequal degrees, for every properly raised human being. In a world with so much to interest, so much to enjoy, and so much also to correct and improve, anyone who has this moderate amount of moral and intellectual equipment is capable of an existence that may be called enviable. Unless such a person, through bad laws or subjection to others' will, is denied the freedom to use the sources of happiness within his reach, he will not fail to find this enviable existence — provided he escapes the positive evils of life, the great sources of physical and mental suffering, such as poverty, disease, and the unkindness, worthlessness, or premature loss of those he loves. The main weight of the problem, therefore, lies in the struggle with these calamities, from which it is rare good fortune to escape entirely, which under present conditions cannot be averted, and often cannot be reduced in any material degree. Yet no one whose opinion deserves a moment's consideration can doubt that most of the great positive evils of the world are in themselves removable, and will, if human affairs continue to improve, eventually be reduced within narrow limits. Poverty, in any sense that involves suffering, may be completely abolished by the wisdom of society combined with the good sense and foresight of individuals. Even disease, that most stubborn of enemies, can be indefinitely reduced by good physical and moral education and proper control of harmful influences, while the progress of science holds out the promise of still more direct conquests over this hateful foe. Every advance in that direction relieves us not only from some of the chances that cut short our own lives, but, even more importantly, from those that deprive us of the people in whom our happiness is wrapped up. As for reversals of fortune and other disappointments connected with worldly circumstances, these are mainly the effect of either gross imprudence, ill-regulated desires, or bad or imperfect social institutions. All the grand sources, in short, of human suffering are to a great degree, many of them almost entirely, conquerable by human care and effort. Their removal is painfully slow — a long succession of generations will perish in the breach before the conquest is complete and this world becomes everything that, if will and knowledge were not lacking, it might easily be made — yet every mind sufficiently intelligent and generous to bear a part, however small and inconspicuous, in the effort will draw a noble enjoyment from the struggle itself, which he would not consent to be without for any bribe in the form of selfish indulgence.

2.14.oldText: And this leads to a fair estimate of what the objectors say about the possibility, and the obligation, of learning to do without happiness. Without question it is possible to do without happiness: it is done involuntarily by nineteen-twentieths of mankind, even in the parts of our present world least sunk in barbarism, and it often has to be done voluntarily by the hero or the martyr, for the sake of something he values more than his own happiness. But what is that something, unless the happiness of others, or some of the means to happiness? It is noble to be capable of giving up one's own share of happiness, or chance of it, entirely; but in the end this self-sacrifice must be for some end — it is not its own end. And if we are told that its end is not happiness but virtue, which is better than happiness, I ask: would the sacrifice be made if the hero or martyr did not believe it would secure for others immunity from similar sacrifices? Would it be made if he thought his renunciation of his own happiness would produce no fruit for any of his fellow creatures, except to make their lot like his and place them in the same condition of having renounced happiness? All honour to those who can give up the personal enjoyment of life when by such renunciation they worthily contribute to increasing the amount of happiness in the world; but anyone who does it, or claims to do it, for any other purpose deserves no more admiration than the ascetic perched on his pillar. He may be an inspiring proof of what people can do, but certainly not an example of what they should do.

2.15.oldText: Though it is only in a very imperfect state of the world's arrangements that anyone can best serve the happiness of others by the absolute sacrifice of his own, yet so long as the world is in that imperfect state, I fully acknowledge that the willingness to make such a sacrifice is the highest virtue that can be found in a human being. I would add that in this condition of the world, paradoxical as it may sound, the conscious ability to do without happiness gives the best prospect of attaining whatever happiness is attainable. For nothing except that consciousness can lift a person above the chances of life by making him feel that, whatever fate and fortune do to him, they cannot subdue him. Once that is felt, it frees him from excessive anxiety about life's evils and enables him, like many a Stoic in the worst times of the Roman Empire, to cultivate in tranquillity the sources of satisfaction available to him, without worrying about the uncertainty of their duration, any more than about their inevitable end.

2.16.oldText: Meanwhile, let utilitarians never stop claiming the morality of self-devotion as a possession that belongs to them by as good a right as it does to the Stoic or the Transcendentalist. The utilitarian morality does recognise in human beings the power to sacrifice their own greatest good for the good of others. It only refuses to admit that the sacrifice is itself a good. A sacrifice that does not increase, or tend to increase, the total sum of happiness it considers wasted. The only self-renunciation it applauds is devotion to the happiness, or to some of the means of happiness, of others — either of mankind collectively or of individuals within the limits set by the collective interests of mankind.

2.17.oldText: I must repeat once more what the assailants of utilitarianism rarely have the fairness to acknowledge: that the happiness which forms the utilitarian standard of right conduct is not the agent's own happiness, but the happiness of all concerned. As between his own happiness and that of others, utilitarianism requires him to be as strictly impartial as a disinterested and benevolent spectator. In the golden rule of Jesus of Nazareth we read the complete spirit of the ethics of utility. To do as one would be done by, and to love one's neighbour as oneself, constitute the ideal perfection of utilitarian morality. As the means of coming as close as possible to this ideal, utility would prescribe, first, that laws and social arrangements should place the happiness — or, as practically speaking it may be called, the interest — of every individual as nearly as possible in harmony with the interest of the whole. Secondly, that education and opinion, which have such enormous power over human character, should use that power to establish in the mind of every individual an indissoluble association between his own happiness and the good of the whole, especially between his own happiness and the practice of those modes of conduct, negative and positive, which regard for the universal happiness prescribes. So that not only would he be unable to conceive the possibility of happiness for himself in any way at odds with the general good, but also a direct impulse to promote the general good would be one of every individual's habitual motives of action, and the feelings connected with it would fill a large and prominent place in every human being's conscious life. If those who attack the utilitarian morality represented it to themselves in this, its true character, I do not know what feature possessed by any other morality they could possibly claim it lacks: what more beautiful or more exalted developments of human nature any other ethical system can be supposed to foster, or what springs of action unavailable to the utilitarian such systems rely on to put their commands into effect.

2.18.oldText: The objectors to utilitarianism cannot always be accused of representing it in an unflattering light. On the contrary, those of them who hold anything like a fair idea of its disinterested character sometimes object that its standard is too high for humanity. They say it is asking too much to require people to act always from the motive of promoting the general interests of society. But this is to mistake the very meaning of a moral standard and to confuse the rule of action with the motive for it. It is the business of ethics to tell us what our duties are, or by what test we may know them; but no system of ethics requires that the sole motive of all we do be a sense of duty. On the contrary, ninety-nine hundredths of all our actions are done from other motives, and rightly so, if the rule of duty does not condemn them. It is all the more unjust to utilitarianism that this particular misunderstanding should be used as an objection to it, since utilitarian moralists have gone further than almost anyone else in affirming that the motive has nothing to do with the morality of the action, though much to do with the worth of the agent. He who saves a fellow creature from drowning does what is morally right, whether his motive is duty or the hope of being paid for his trouble. He who betrays the friend who trusts him is guilty of a crime, even if his aim is to serve another friend to whom he is under greater obligations.[B] But to speak only of actions done from a sense of duty, and in direct obedience to principle: it is a misunderstanding of the utilitarian mode of thought to conceive of it as requiring people to fix their minds on so vast a generality as the world, or society at large. The great majority of good actions are aimed not at the benefit of the world but at the benefit of individuals, of which the good of the world is composed. The thoughts of the most virtuous person on those occasions need not travel beyond the particular people concerned, except so far as is necessary to assure himself that in benefiting them he is not violating the rights — that is, the legitimate and authorised expectations — of anyone else. The multiplication of happiness is, according to utilitarian ethics, the object of virtue. The occasions on which any person (except one in a thousand) has the power to do this on an extended scale — in other words, to be a public benefactor — are exceptional, and only on those occasions is he called on to consider public utility. In every other case, private utility — the interest or happiness of some few people — is all he has to attend to. Only those whose actions have an influence on society at large need habitually concern themselves with so wide an object. In the case of abstaining — of things people forbear to do from moral considerations, even though the consequences in the particular case might be beneficial — it would be unworthy of an intelligent agent not to be consciously aware that the action belongs to a class which, if generally practised, would be generally harmful, and that this is the ground of the obligation to abstain. The amount of regard for the public interest implied in this recognition is no greater than every system of morals demands, since they all require us to abstain from whatever is plainly damaging to society.

2.19.oldText: The same considerations dispose of another reproach against the doctrine of utility, founded on a still grosser misconception of the purpose of a moral standard, and of the very meaning of the words right and wrong. It is often claimed that utilitarianism makes people cold and unsympathetic, chills their moral feelings towards individuals, and makes them focus only on the dry and hard consideration of the consequences of actions, ignoring in their moral assessment the qualities from which those actions spring. If the claim means that they do not allow their judgment of an action's rightness or wrongness to be influenced by their opinion of the person doing it, this is a complaint not against utilitarianism but against having any moral standard at all. No known ethical standard decides that an action is good or bad because it is done by a good or bad person, much less because it is done by an amiable, brave, or benevolent person — or the opposite. These considerations are relevant not to evaluating actions, but to evaluating persons. There is nothing in the utilitarian theory inconsistent with the fact that there are other things which interest us in people besides the rightness or wrongness of their actions. The Stoics, indeed, with the paradoxical misuse of language that was part of their system and by which they tried to lift themselves above any concern except virtue, were fond of saying that whoever has virtue has everything — that he, and only he, is rich, beautiful, a king. But the utilitarian doctrine makes no such claim for the virtuous person. Utilitarians are perfectly aware that there are other desirable possessions and qualities besides virtue, and are perfectly willing to grant them all their full worth. They are also aware that a right action does not necessarily indicate a virtuous character, and that actions deserving blame often come from qualities that deserve praise. When this is clear in a particular case, it modifies their estimate, not of the act, but of the agent. I grant that they are nonetheless of the opinion that in the long run the best proof of a good character is good actions, and they firmly refuse to consider as good any mental disposition whose predominant tendency is to produce bad conduct. This makes them unpopular with many people, but it is an unpopularity they must share with anyone who takes the distinction between right and wrong seriously, and the reproach is not one that a conscientious utilitarian need be anxious to deflect.

2.20.oldText: If the objection means no more than that many utilitarians look at the morality of actions, measured by the utilitarian standard, with too narrow a focus, and do not give enough weight to the other beauties of character which go into making a human being lovable or admirable, this may be granted. Utilitarians who have cultivated their moral feelings but not their sympathies or artistic perceptions do fall into this mistake, and so do all other moralists under the same conditions. What can be said in excuse for other moralists applies equally to them: that if there is to be any error, it is better that it should be on that side. As a matter of fact, we may affirm that among utilitarians, as among the adherents of other systems, there is every conceivable degree of strictness and laxity in applying their standard. Some are even puritanically rigorous, while others are as indulgent as any sinner or sentimentalist could wish. But on the whole, a doctrine that places the interest mankind has in suppressing and preventing conduct which violates the moral law front and centre is unlikely to be inferior to any other in turning the sanctions of opinion against such violations. It is true that the question of what does violate the moral law is one on which those who accept different standards of morality are likely now and then to differ. But moral disagreement was not first brought into the world by utilitarianism, while utilitarianism does supply, if not always an easy method, at least a tangible and intelligible way of deciding such disagreements.

2.21.oldText: It may be worth noting a few more of the common misconceptions of utilitarian ethics, even those so obvious and gross that one might think no candid and intelligent person could fall into them. People, even of considerable mental ability, often give themselves so little trouble to understand the implications of any opinion they have a prejudice against, and are generally so unaware of this voluntary ignorance as a defect, that the crudest misunderstandings of ethical doctrines are constantly to be met with in the deliberate writings of people who lay great claim both to high principle and to philosophy. It is not uncommon to hear the doctrine of utility denounced as a godless doctrine. If it is necessary to say anything at all against so bare an assertion, we may say that the question depends on what idea we have formed of the moral character of God. If we truly believe that God desires, above all things, the happiness of his creatures, and that this was his purpose in creating them, then utility is not only not godless but more profoundly religious than any other doctrine. If it is meant that utilitarianism does not recognise the revealed will of God as the supreme law of morals, I answer that a utilitarian who believes in the perfect goodness and wisdom of God necessarily believes that whatever God has seen fit to reveal on the subject of morals must fulfil the requirements of utility to a supreme degree. But others besides utilitarians have held the opinion that the Christian revelation was intended, and is suited, to imbue the hearts and minds of humankind with a spirit that would enable them to find for themselves what is right and incline them to do it when found — rather than to tell them, except in a very general way, what it is — and that we need a doctrine of ethics, carefully worked out, to interpret God's will to us. Whether that view is correct or not, it is unnecessary to discuss here, since whatever help religion — whether natural or revealed — can give to ethical inquiry is as open to the utilitarian moralist as to anyone else. He can use it as God's testimony to the usefulness or harmfulness of any given course of action, by as good a right as others can use it for the indication of a transcendental law that has no connection with usefulness or with happiness.

2.22.oldText: Again, Utility is often summarily stigmatised as an immoral doctrine by giving it the name of Expediency and exploiting the popular use of that term to contrast it with Principle. But the Expedient, in the sense in which it is opposed to the Right, generally means that which is expedient for the particular interest of the agent himself — as when a minister sacrifices the interest of his country to keep himself in office. When it means anything better than this, it means that which is expedient for some immediate object, some temporary purpose, but which violates a rule whose observance is expedient to a much higher degree. The Expedient, in this sense, instead of being the same thing as the useful, is a branch of the harmful. Thus, it would often be expedient, in order to get out of some momentary embarrassment, or to attain some object immediately useful to ourselves or others, to tell a lie. But inasmuch as cultivating in ourselves a keen sensitivity on the subject of truthfulness is one of the most useful things our conduct can produce, and weakening that feeling is one of the most harmful — and inasmuch as any deviation from truth, even unintentional, does that much towards weakening the trustworthiness of human assertion (which is not only the principal support of all present social well-being but whose insufficiency does more than any one thing that can be named to hold back civilisation, virtue, everything on which human happiness on the largest scale depends) — we feel that violating, for a present advantage, a rule of such transcendent expediency is not expedient, and that anyone who, for the sake of a convenience to himself or to some other individual, does what he can to deprive mankind of the good, and inflict on them the evil, involved in the greater or lesser reliance they can place on one another's word, acts as one of their worst enemies. Yet even this rule, sacred as it is, admits of possible exceptions, as all moralists acknowledge. The chief such exception is when withholding some fact (such as information from an evildoer, or bad news from a person dangerously ill) would save someone (especially someone other than oneself) from great and undeserved evil, and when withholding can only be effected by denial. But in order that the exception may not extend itself beyond what is needed, and may have the least possible effect in weakening reliance on truthfulness, it ought to be recognised, and, if possible, its limits defined. If the principle of utility is good for anything, it must be good for weighing these conflicting utilities against one another and marking out the region within which one or the other predominates.

2.23.oldText: Again, defenders of utility often find themselves called upon to answer objections like this: that there is not time, before acting, to calculate and weigh the effects of any line of conduct on the general happiness. This is exactly as if someone were to say that it is impossible to guide one's conduct by Christianity, because there is not time, on every occasion when something has to be done, to read through the Old and New Testaments. The answer to the objection is that there has been ample time, namely the whole past duration of the human species. During all that time, mankind has been learning by experience the tendencies of actions, and on that experience all the prudence as well as all the morality of life depends. People talk as if this course of experience had so far been put off, and as if at the moment some man feels tempted to interfere with another's property or life, he had to begin considering for the first time whether murder and theft are harmful to human happiness. Even then I do not think he would find the question very puzzling, but at any rate the matter is now done for him. It is truly a whimsical supposition that if mankind agreed to take utility as the test of morality, they would remain without any agreement on what is useful, and would take no steps to have their notions on the subject taught to the young and enforced by law and opinion. There is no difficulty in proving any ethical standard whatever to work badly, if we suppose universal idiocy to go with it; but on any hypothesis short of that, mankind must by this time have acquired positive beliefs about the effects of some actions on their happiness. The beliefs that have thus been handed down are the rules of morality for the multitude, and for the philosopher too, until he has succeeded in finding better. That philosophers could easily do this, even now, on many subjects; that the received code of ethics is by no means divinely ordained; and that mankind still has much to learn about the effects of actions on the general happiness — I admit, or rather, I earnestly maintain. The corollaries of the principle of utility, like the precepts of every practical art, admit of indefinite improvement, and in a progressive state of the human mind their improvement is perpetually going on. But to consider the rules of morality as improvable is one thing; to skip over the intermediate generalisations entirely and try to test each individual action directly by the first principle is another. It is a strange notion that the acknowledgment of a first principle is inconsistent with the admission of secondary ones. To tell a traveller where his final destination is is not to forbid the use of landmarks and signposts along the way. The proposition that happiness is the end and aim of morality does not mean that no road ought to be laid down to that goal, or that people going there should not be advised to take one direction rather than another. People really ought to leave off talking the kind of nonsense on this subject that they would neither talk nor listen to on other matters of practical concern. Nobody argues that the art of navigation is not founded on astronomy because sailors cannot wait to calculate the Nautical Almanac. Being rational creatures, they go to sea with it ready-calculated, and all rational creatures go out on the sea of life with their minds made up on the common questions of right and wrong, as well as on many of the far more difficult questions of wise and foolish. As long as foresight is a human quality, they may be presumed to continue doing so. Whatever we adopt as the fundamental principle of morality, we need subordinate principles to apply it. The impossibility of doing without them, being common to all systems, can be no argument against any one in particular; but to argue gravely as if no such secondary principles were available, and as if mankind had remained until now, and always must remain, without drawing any general conclusions from the experience of human life, is, I think, as high a pitch as absurdity has ever reached in philosophical controversy.

2.24.oldText: The remainder of the stock arguments against utilitarianism mostly consist in charging it with the common weaknesses of human nature and the general difficulties that beset conscientious people in shaping their course through life. We are told that a utilitarian will be apt to make his own particular case an exception to moral rules, and, when under temptation, will see more utility in breaking a rule than in keeping it. But is utility the only creed capable of furnishing us with excuses for wrongdoing, and ways of cheating our own conscience? They are supplied in abundance by every doctrine that recognises as a fact in morals the existence of conflicting considerations — which every doctrine does, that any sane person has ever believed. It is not the fault of any creed, but of the complicated nature of human affairs, that rules of conduct cannot be so framed as to need no exceptions, and that hardly any kind of action can safely be laid down as either always obligatory or always condemnable. There is no ethical creed that does not soften the rigidity of its laws by giving a certain latitude, under the moral responsibility of the agent, for accommodation to peculiarities of circumstance. And under every creed, through the opening thus made, self-deception and dishonest casuistry get in. There is no moral system under which clear cases of conflicting obligation do not arise. These are the real difficulties, the knotty points in both the theory of ethics and the conscientious guidance of personal conduct. They are dealt with in practice with greater or less success depending on the intellect and virtue of the individual; but it can hardly be claimed that anyone will be less qualified to deal with them by having an ultimate standard to which conflicting rights and duties can be referred. If utility is the ultimate source of moral obligations, utility may be invoked to decide between them when their demands are incompatible. Though applying the standard may be difficult, it is better than having none at all. In other systems, where the moral laws all claim independent authority, there is no common umpire entitled to step in between them. Their claims to precedence over one another rest on little better than sophistry, and unless they are decided, as they generally are, by the unacknowledged influence of considerations of utility, they leave free scope for the action of personal desires and partialities. We must remember that it is only in such cases of conflict between secondary principles that first principles need to be appealed to. There is no case of moral obligation in which some secondary principle is not involved, and if only one is involved, there can rarely be any real doubt in the mind of any person who recognises the principle itself which one it is.

2.25.oldText: [Footnote A: The author of this essay has reason for believing himself to be the first person who brought the word utilitarian into use. He did not invent it but adopted it from a passing expression in Mr. Galt's Annals of the Parish. After using it as a designation for several years, he and others dropped it from a growing dislike to anything resembling a badge or watchword of sectarian distinction. But as a name for one single opinion, not a set of opinions — to denote the recognition of utility as a standard, not any particular way of applying it — the term fills a gap in the language, and offers, in many cases, a convenient way of avoiding tiresome circumlocution.]

But the motive — that is, the feeling that makes him will to do it — when it makes no difference in the act, makes none in the morality, though it makes a great difference in our moral estimation of the agent, especially if it indicates a good or a bad habitual disposition — a bent of character from which useful, or from which hurtful, actions are likely to arise.]

3.0.oldText: The question is often asked, and rightly so, about any supposed moral standard: What is its sanction? What are the motives to obey it? Or more specifically: what is the source of its obligation? Where does its binding force come from? It is a necessary part of moral philosophy to answer this question. Though it often takes the shape of an objection to utilitarian morality — as if it had some special bearing on that doctrine over others — it really arises in relation to all standards. In fact, it comes up whenever a person is asked to adopt a standard, or to ground morality on a basis he has not been used to resting it on. For the customary morality — the one consecrated by education and opinion — is the only one that presents itself to the mind with the feeling of being in itself obligatory. When a person is asked to believe that this morality derives its obligation from some general principle around which custom has not thrown the same halo, the claim strikes him as a paradox. The supposed corollaries seem to him to have more binding force than the original theorem; the superstructure seems to stand better without than with what is presented as its foundation. He says to himself: I feel that I am bound not to rob or murder, betray or deceive. But why am I bound to promote the general happiness? If my own happiness lies in something else, why may I not give that the preference?

3.1.oldText: If the view that utilitarian philosophy takes of the nature of the moral sense is correct, this difficulty will always arise — until the influences that form moral character have taken as firm a hold of the principle as they have of some of its consequences. That is, until, through better education, the feeling of unity with our fellow creatures becomes (what we cannot doubt Christ intended it to be) as deeply rooted in our character, and as completely a part of our nature in our own consciousness, as the horror of crime is in a normally well-brought-up young person. Meanwhile, however, the difficulty has no peculiar application to the doctrine of utility, but is inherent in every attempt to analyse morality and reduce it to principles. Unless the principle is already invested in people's minds with as much sacredness as any of its applications, the analysis always seems to strip those applications of part of their sanctity.

3.2.oldText: The principle of utility either has, or there is no reason why it might not have, all the sanctions that belong to any other system of morals. Those sanctions are either external or internal. The external ones do not need to be discussed at length. They are the hope of favour and the fear of displeasure from our fellow creatures or from the Ruler of the Universe, along with whatever we have of sympathy or affection for them, or of love and awe of Him, inclining us to do His will independently of selfish consequences. There is clearly no reason why all these motives for compliance should not attach themselves to the utilitarian morality as fully and powerfully as to any other. Indeed, those motives that refer to our fellow creatures are bound to do so in proportion to the amount of general intelligence; because whether or not there is any other ground of moral obligation than the general happiness, people do desire happiness, and however imperfect their own practice may be, they desire and approve of all conduct in others towards them by which they think their happiness is promoted. As for the religious motive: if people believe, as most profess to do, in God's goodness, then those who think that promoting the general happiness is the essence — or even just the criterion — of good must necessarily believe that this is also what God approves. The whole force, therefore, of external reward and punishment, whether physical or moral, whether coming from God or from our fellow human beings, together with all that human nature is capable of in the way of disinterested devotion to either, becomes available to enforce the utilitarian morality, in proportion as that morality is recognised — and the more powerfully, the more the resources of education and general cultivation are bent to the purpose.

3.3.oldText: So much for external sanctions. The internal sanction of duty, whatever our standard of duty may be, is one and the same: a feeling in our own mind, a pain, more or less intense, attendant on the violation of duty, which in properly cultivated moral natures rises, in the more serious cases, to a recoil from violation as something impossible. This feeling, when disinterested and connecting itself with the pure idea of duty — and not with some particular form of it, or with any of the merely accessory circumstances — is the essence of Conscience. In that complex phenomenon as it actually exists, however, the simple fact is generally encrusted with collateral associations, drawn from sympathy, from love, and still more from fear; from all the forms of religious feeling; from the memories of childhood and of our whole past life; from self-esteem, from desire for the esteem of others, and occasionally even from self-abasement. This extreme complication is, I think, the origin of the sort of mystical character which, by a tendency of the human mind of which there are many other examples, is apt to be attributed to the idea of moral obligation. It leads people to believe that the idea cannot possibly attach itself to any other objects than those which, by some supposed mysterious law, are found in our present experience to excite it. Its binding force, however, consists in the existence of a mass of feeling that has to be broken through in order to do what violates our standard of right, and which, if we do violate that standard, will probably have to be encountered afterwards in the form of remorse. Whatever theory we hold about the nature or origin of conscience, this is what essentially constitutes it.

3.4.oldText: The ultimate sanction, therefore, of all morality (external motives aside) being a subjective feeling in our own minds, I see nothing embarrassing for those whose standard is utility in the question: what is the sanction of that particular standard? We may answer: the same as for all other moral standards — the conscientious feelings of mankind. Undoubtedly this sanction has no binding force on those who lack the feelings it appeals to; but those people will not be any more obedient to any other moral principle than to the utilitarian one. Morality of any kind has no hold on them except through the external sanctions. Meanwhile the feelings exist, as a fact of human nature, and the reality of these feelings — and the great power with which they can act on those in whom they have been duly cultivated — is proved by experience. No reason has ever been shown why they cannot be cultivated to as great intensity in connection with the utilitarian rule of morals as with any other.

3.5.oldText: There is, I am aware, a tendency to believe that a person who sees in moral obligation a transcendental fact, an objective reality belonging to the province of "Things in themselves," is likely to be more obedient to it than someone who believes it to be entirely subjective, having its seat only in human consciousness. But whatever a person's opinion on this point of Ontology, the force he is really driven by is his own subjective feeling, and is exactly measured by its strength. No one's belief that Duty is an objective reality is stronger than the belief that God is one; yet belief in God, apart from the expectation of actual reward and punishment, operates on conduct only through, and in proportion to, the subjective religious feeling. The sanction, so far as it is disinterested, is always in the mind itself. The notion of the transcendental moralists must therefore be that this sanction will not exist in the mind unless it is believed to have its root outside the mind; and that if a person can say to himself, "What is restraining me, and what is called my conscience, is only a feeling in my own mind," he may possibly conclude that when the feeling stops, the obligation stops, and that if he finds the feeling inconvenient he may disregard it and try to get rid of it. But is this danger confined to the utilitarian morality? Does the belief that moral obligation has its seat outside the mind make the feeling of it too strong to be got rid of? In fact, the opposite is so much the case that all moralists admit, and lament, the ease with which in most minds conscience can be silenced or stifled. The question "Need I obey my conscience?" is asked just as often by people who have never heard of the principle of utility as by its adherents. Those whose conscientious feelings are weak enough to allow them to ask this question will, if they answer it affirmatively, not do so because they believe in the transcendental theory, but because of the external sanctions.

3.6.oldText: For our present purpose it is not necessary to decide whether the feeling of duty is innate or implanted. Assuming it to be innate, it is an open question to what objects it naturally attaches itself, because the philosophical supporters of that theory are now agreed that the intuitive perception is of principles of morality, not of details. If there is anything innate in the matter, I see no reason why the feeling that is innate should not be regard for the pleasures and pains of others. If there is any moral principle which is intuitively obligatory, I would say it must be that one. If so, intuitive ethics would coincide with utilitarian ethics, and there would be no further quarrel between them. Even as things stand, the intuitive moralists, though they believe there are other intuitive moral obligations, already believe this is one of them, since they unanimously hold that a large part of morality turns on the consideration due to the interests of our fellow creatures. So if belief in the transcendental origin of moral obligation gives any extra power to the internal sanction, it seems to me that the utilitarian principle already has the benefit of it.

3.7.oldText: On the other hand, if, as I myself believe, the moral feelings are not innate but acquired, they are no less natural for that. It is natural for human beings to speak, to reason, to build cities, to cultivate the ground, though these are acquired capacities. The moral feelings are not, indeed, part of our nature in the sense of being present to any perceptible degree in all of us; but this, unhappily, is a fact admitted by those who most strongly believe in their transcendental origin. Like the other acquired capacities just mentioned, the moral faculty, if not a part of our nature, is a natural outgrowth from it. Like them, it is capable, to a small degree, of springing up spontaneously, and capable of being brought by cultivation to a high degree of development. Unhappily it is also capable, by sufficient use of the external sanctions and the force of early impressions, of being cultivated in almost any direction, so that there is hardly anything so absurd or so harmful that it cannot, by means of these influences, be made to act on the human mind with all the authority of conscience. To doubt that the same power could be given by the same means to the principle of utility, even if it had no foundation in human nature, would be to fly in the face of all experience.

3.8.oldText: But moral associations that are wholly artificial yield by degrees, as intellectual culture progresses, to the dissolving force of analysis. If the feeling of duty, when associated with utility, would seem equally arbitrary; if there were no leading department of our nature, no powerful class of sentiments, with which that association would harmonise — sentiments that would make us feel it congenial and incline us not only to foster it in others (for which we have plenty of interested motives), but also to cherish it in ourselves — if, in short, there were no natural basis of sentiment for utilitarian morality, then it might well happen that this association too, even after it had been implanted by education, could be analysed away.

3.9.oldText: But this basis of powerful natural sentiment does exist, and it is this which, once the general happiness is recognised as the ethical standard, will constitute the strength of the utilitarian morality. This firm foundation is the social feelings of mankind — the desire to be in unity with our fellow creatures — which is already a powerful principle in human nature, and happily one of those that tend to grow stronger, even without explicit teaching, under the influence of advancing civilisation. The social state is at once so natural, so necessary, and so habitual to human beings that, except in some unusual circumstances or by an effort of voluntary abstraction, no one ever conceives of himself except as a member of a body. This association is riveted more and more firmly the further mankind moves from a state of savage independence. Any condition, therefore, that is essential to a state of society becomes more and more an inseparable part of every person's conception of the state of things into which he is born, and which is the destiny of a human being. Now, society between human beings, except in the relation of master and slave, is clearly impossible on any other footing than that the interests of all are to be considered. Society between equals can only exist on the understanding that the interests of all are to be regarded equally. And since in every state of civilisation everyone except an absolute monarch has equals, everyone has to live on these terms with somebody, and in every age some advance is made towards a state in which it will be impossible to live permanently on other terms with anybody. In this way people grow up unable to imagine as possible for themselves a state of total disregard of others' interests. They are obliged to picture themselves as at least abstaining from all the grosser injuries, and (if only for their own protection) living in a state of constant protest against them. They are also familiar with the fact of cooperating with others, and setting themselves a collective, not an individual, interest as the aim (at least for the time being) of their actions. So long as they are cooperating, their ends are identified with those of others — there is at least a temporary feeling that the interests of others are their own interests. Not only does every strengthening of social ties, and every healthy growth of society, give each individual a stronger personal interest in actively consulting others' welfare; it also leads him to identify his feelings more and more with their good, or at least with an ever greater degree of practical regard for it. He comes, as if instinctively, to be conscious of himself as a being who, of course, pays regard to others. The good of others becomes for him something naturally and necessarily to be attended to, like any of the physical conditions of our existence. Now, whatever amount of this feeling a person has, he is driven by the strongest motives, both of interest and of sympathy, to display it, and as far as he can to encourage it in others; and even if he has none of it himself, he is just as interested as anyone else that others should have it. Consequently, the smallest seeds of this feeling are caught hold of and nourished by the contagion of sympathy and the influences of education, and a complete web of supporting associations is woven around it by the powerful agency of the external sanctions. This way of conceiving ourselves and human life, as civilisation goes on, is felt to be more and more natural. Every step in political improvement makes it more so, by removing sources of opposed interest and levelling those inequalities of legal privilege between individuals or classes, because of which there are large portions of mankind whose happiness it is still possible to disregard. In an improving state of the human mind, the influences are constantly increasing that tend to generate in each individual a feeling of unity with all the rest — a feeling which, if perfect, would make him never think of, or desire, any beneficial condition for himself in whose benefits others were not included. If we now suppose this feeling of unity to be taught as a religion, and the whole force of education, institutions, and opinion directed, as once happened in the case of religion, to make every person grow up from infancy surrounded on all sides by both the profession and the practice of it, I think no one who can grasp this conception will feel any misgiving about the sufficiency of the ultimate sanction for the Happiness morality. To any student of ethics who finds the realisation difficult, I recommend, as a way of making it easier, the second of M. Comte's two principal works, the Système de Politique Positive. I have the strongest objections to the system of politics and morals set out in that treatise, but I think it has more than abundantly shown the possibility of giving to the service of humanity, even without the help of belief in a Providence, both the physical power and the social efficacy of a religion — making it take hold of human life and colour all thought, feeling, and action in a way of which the greatest ascendancy ever exercised by any religion may be only a type and foretaste. Its danger is not that it should be insufficient, but that it should be so excessive as to interfere unduly with human freedom and individuality.

3.10.oldText: Nor is it necessary, for the feeling that constitutes the binding force of utilitarian morality on those who recognise it, to wait for the social influences that would make its obligation felt by mankind at large. In the comparatively early state of human advancement in which we now live, a person cannot indeed feel that entire sympathy with all others which would make any real discord in the general direction of their conduct of life impossible. But already a person in whom the social feeling is at all developed cannot bring himself to think of the rest of his fellow creatures as struggling rivals with him for the means of happiness, whom he must want to see defeated in their aim so that he may succeed in his. The deeply rooted conception that every individual even now has of himself as a social being tends to make him feel it one of his natural wants that there should be harmony between his feelings and aims and those of his fellow creatures. If differences of opinion and of mental culture make it impossible for him to share many of their actual feelings — perhaps even make him denounce and defy those feelings — he still needs to be conscious that his real aim and theirs do not conflict; that he is not opposing what they really want, namely their own good, but is, on the contrary, promoting it. This feeling in most individuals is much weaker than their selfish feelings, and is often missing altogether. But to those who have it, it has all the characteristics of a natural feeling. It does not present itself to their minds as a superstition of upbringing, or as a law despotically imposed by the power of society, but as an attribute they would be the worse for being without. This conviction is the ultimate sanction of the greatest-happiness morality. It is this which makes any mind of well-developed feelings work with, rather than against, the outward motives to care for others provided by what I have called the external sanctions. And when those sanctions are lacking, or pull in the opposite direction, this conviction in itself constitutes a powerful internal binding force, in proportion to the sensitiveness and thoughtfulness of the character — since few but those whose mind is a moral blank could bear to lay out their course of life on the plan of paying no regard to others except so far as their own private interest compels.

4.0.oldText: It has already been pointed out that questions of ultimate ends do not admit of proof in the ordinary sense of the word.
