Being incapable of proof by reasoning is common to all first principles — to the first premises of our knowledge as well as those of our conduct. But the former, being matters of fact, can be the subject of a direct appeal to the faculties that judge of fact, namely our senses and our internal consciousness. Can an appeal be made to the same faculties on questions of practical ends? Or by what other faculty are they known to us?

4.1.oldText: Questions about ends are, in other words, questions about what things are desirable. The utilitarian doctrine is that happiness is desirable, and the only thing desirable, as an end — all other things being desirable only as means to that end. What must be required of this doctrine — what conditions must it fulfil — to make good its claim to be believed?

4.2.oldText: The only proof that can be given that an object is visible is that people actually see it. The only proof that a sound is audible is that people hear it — and so with the other sources of our experience. In the same way, I think, the only evidence it is possible to produce that anything is desirable is that people do actually desire it. If the end which the utilitarian doctrine proposes for itself were not, in theory and in practice, acknowledged to be an end, nothing could ever convince any person that it was. No reason can be given why the general happiness is desirable, except that each person, so far as he believes it to be attainable, desires his own happiness. This being a fact, however, we have not only all the proof the case admits of, but all it is possible to require, that happiness is a good: that each person's happiness is a good to that person, and the general happiness, therefore, a good to the aggregate of all persons. Happiness has made out its title as one of the ends of conduct, and consequently one of the criteria of morality.

4.3.oldText: But this alone has not shown happiness to be the sole criterion. To do that, it would seem necessary, by the same rule, to show not only that people desire happiness, but that they never desire anything else. Now it is obvious that they do desire things which, in common language, are decidedly distinguished from happiness. They desire, for example, virtue, and the absence of vice, no less truly than pleasure and the absence of pain. The desire for virtue is not as universal, but it is as authentic a fact as the desire for happiness. Hence the opponents of the utilitarian standard think they have the right to infer that there are other ends of human action besides happiness, and that happiness is not the standard of approval and disapproval.

4.4.oldText: But does the utilitarian doctrine deny that people desire virtue, or maintain that virtue is not a thing to be desired? Quite the opposite. It maintains not only that virtue is to be desired, but that it is to be desired disinterestedly, for its own sake. Whatever the opinion of utilitarian moralists may be about the original conditions which make virtue virtue; however much they may believe (as they do) that actions and dispositions are virtuous only because they promote some other end than virtue itself; once that is granted, and once it has been decided, on considerations of this kind, what is virtuous, they not only place virtue at the very head of the things that are good as means to the ultimate end, but they also recognise as a psychological fact the possibility of its being, for the individual, a good in itself, without looking to any end beyond it. They hold that the mind is not in a right state — not in a state conformable to Utility, not in the state most conducive to the general happiness — unless it does love virtue in this way: as a thing desirable in itself, even if, in a particular case, it should not produce those other desirable consequences which it tends to produce, and on account of which it is held to be virtue. This opinion is in no way a departure from the Happiness principle. The ingredients of happiness are very various, and each of them is desirable in itself, and not merely when considered as adding to a total. The principle of utility does not mean that any given pleasure — music, for example — or any given freedom from pain — health, for example — is to be looked on as a means to a collective something called happiness, and to be desired on that account. They are desired, and are desirable, in and for themselves. Besides being means, they are part of the end. Virtue, according to utilitarian doctrine, is not naturally and originally part of the end, but it is capable of becoming so — and in those who love it disinterestedly it has become so, and is desired and cherished, not as a means to happiness, but as a part of their happiness.

4.5.oldText: To illustrate this further, we may recall that virtue is not the only thing which is originally a means and which, if it were not a means to anything else, would be and remain a matter of indifference, but which through association with what it is a means to comes to be desired for itself, and that with the utmost intensity. Take, for example, the love of money. There is nothing originally more desirable about money than about any heap of glittering pebbles. Its worth is solely that of the things it will buy — the desires for other things than itself which it is the means of gratifying. Yet the love of money is not only one of the strongest moving forces of human life, but money is, in many cases, desired in and for itself. The desire to possess it is often stronger than the desire to use it, and goes on increasing when all the desires that point to ends beyond it, ends to be reached by it, are falling off. It may then truly be said that money is desired not for the sake of an end, but as part of the end. From being a means to happiness, it has come to be itself a principal ingredient of the individual's conception of happiness. The same may be said of the majority of the great objects of human life — power, for example, or fame — except that to each of these there is a certain amount of immediate pleasure attached, which has at least the appearance of being naturally inherent in them, something that cannot be said of money. Still, the strongest natural attraction both of power and of fame is the immense help they give to attaining our other wishes, and it is the strong association thus generated between them and all our objects of desire that gives the direct desire of them the intensity it often takes on, sometimes surpassing in strength all other desires in certain characters. In these cases, the means have become a part of the end, and a more important part of it than any of the things they are means to. What was once desired as an instrument for attaining happiness has come to be desired for its own sake. Being desired for its own sake, however, it is desired as part of happiness. The person is made — or thinks he would be made — happy by its mere possession, and is made unhappy by failure to obtain it. The desire for it is not something different from the desire for happiness, any more than the love of music or the desire for health is. They are included in happiness. They are some of the elements of which the desire for happiness is composed. Happiness is not an abstract idea but a concrete whole, and these are some of its parts. The utilitarian standard sanctions and approves their being so. Life would be a poor thing, very ill provided with sources of happiness, if there were not this provision of nature by which things originally indifferent, but conducive to, or otherwise associated with, the satisfaction of our primitive desires, become in themselves sources of pleasure more valuable than the primitive pleasures — both in permanence, in the span of human existence they are capable of covering, and even in intensity. Virtue, according to the utilitarian conception, is a good of this kind. There was no original desire for it, or motive to it, except its conduciveness to pleasure, and especially to protection from pain. But through the association so formed, it may be felt as a good in itself, and desired as such with as great intensity as any other good — with this difference between it and the love of money, of power, or of fame, that all of these may, and often do, make the individual harmful to the other members of the society he belongs to, whereas nothing makes him so much a blessing to them as the cultivation of the disinterested love of virtue. Consequently the utilitarian standard, while it tolerates and approves those other acquired desires up to the point beyond which they would be more injurious to the general happiness than promotive of it, enjoins and requires the cultivation of the love of virtue to the greatest strength possible, as being above all things important to the general happiness.

4.6.oldText: It follows from the preceding considerations that there is in reality nothing desired except happiness. Whatever is desired otherwise than as a means to some end beyond itself, and ultimately to happiness, is desired as itself a part of happiness, and is not desired for itself until it has become so. Those who desire virtue for its own sake desire it either because the consciousness of it is a pleasure, or because the consciousness of being without it is a pain, or for both reasons together. In truth, the pleasure and the pain rarely exist separately, but almost always together — the same person feeling pleasure in the degree of virtue attained, and pain in not having attained more. If one of these gave him no pleasure and the other no pain, he would not love or desire virtue, or would desire it only for the other benefits it might produce for himself or for those he cared for.

4.7.oldText: We now have an answer to the question of what kind of proof the principle of utility is susceptible of. If the opinion I have just stated is psychologically true — if human nature is so constituted as to desire nothing which is not either a part of happiness or a means to happiness — we can have no other proof, and we need no other, that these are the only things desirable. If so, happiness is the sole end of human action, and the promotion of it is the test by which to judge of all human conduct; from which it necessarily follows that it must be the criterion of morality, since a part is included in the whole.

4.8.oldText: Now, to decide whether this is really so — whether mankind do desire nothing for itself except what is a pleasure to them, or what the absence of would be a pain — we have evidently arrived at a question of fact and experience, depending, like all such questions, on evidence. It can only be settled by practised self-consciousness and self-observation, assisted by observation of others. I believe that these sources of evidence, impartially consulted, will declare that desiring a thing and finding it pleasant, an aversion to it and thinking of it as painful, are phenomena entirely inseparable, or rather two parts of the same phenomenon — strictly speaking, two different ways of naming the same psychological fact: that to think of an object as desirable (unless for the sake of its consequences) and to think of it as pleasant, are one and the same thing, and that to desire anything except in proportion as the idea of it is pleasant is a physical and metaphysical impossibility.

4.9.oldText: So obvious does this appear to me that I expect it will hardly be disputed. The objection raised will be not that desire can possibly be directed to anything ultimately except pleasure and freedom from pain, but that the will is a different thing from desire — that a person of settled virtue, or anyone else whose purposes are fixed, carries out his purposes without any thought of the pleasure he gets from contemplating them, or expects to get from their fulfilment; and persists in acting on them even when these pleasures are much reduced, by changes in his character or the decay of his passive sensibilities, or are outweighed by the pains the pursuit of the purposes may bring on him. All this I fully admit, and have stated elsewhere as positively and emphatically as anyone. Will, the active phenomenon, is a different thing from desire, the state of passive sensibility. Though originally an offshoot of desire, it may in time take root and detach itself from the parent stock — so much so that in the case of a habitual purpose, instead of willing the thing because we desire it, we often desire it only because we will it. This, however, is just an instance of that familiar fact, the power of habit, and is in no way confined to the case of virtuous actions. Many indifferent things, which people originally did from some motive, they continue to do from habit. Sometimes this is done unconsciously, the consciousness coming only after the action; at other times with conscious volition, but volition which has become habitual, and is put into operation by the force of habit, possibly in opposition to the deliberate preference, as often happens with those who have fallen into habits of vicious or hurtful indulgence. Third and last comes the case in which the habitual act of will in the particular instance is not in contradiction to the general intention prevailing at other times, but in fulfilment of it — as with the person of settled virtue, and with all who pursue deliberately and consistently any determinate end. The distinction between will and desire, understood in this way, is an authentic and highly important psychological fact, but the fact consists solely in this: that will, like all other parts of our constitution, is subject to habit, and that we may will from habit what we no longer desire for itself, or desire only because we will it. It is no less true that will, in the beginning, is entirely produced by desire — including under that term the repelling influence of pain as well as the attractive influence of pleasure. Let us now consider, not the person who has a settled will to do right, but the one in whom that virtuous will is still feeble, conquerable by temptation, and not to be fully relied on. By what means can it be strengthened? How can the will to be virtuous, where it does not exist in sufficient strength, be implanted or awakened? Only by making the person desire virtue — by making him think of it in a pleasurable light, or of its absence in a painful one. It is by associating doing right with pleasure, or doing wrong with pain, or by eliciting and impressing and bringing home to the person's experience the pleasure naturally involved in the one or the pain in the other, that it is possible to call forth that will to be virtuous which, once settled, acts without any thought of either pleasure or pain. Will is the child of desire, and passes out of the dominion of its parent only to come under that of habit. What is the result of habit affords no presumption of being intrinsically good, and there would be no reason for wishing that the purpose of virtue should become independent of pleasure and pain, were it not that the influence of the pleasurable and painful associations which prompt to virtue is not sufficiently to be relied on for unerring constancy of action until it has acquired the support of habit. In feeling as in conduct, habit is the only thing that imparts certainty. It is because of the importance to others of being able to rely absolutely on one's feelings and conduct, and to oneself of being able to rely on one's own, that the will to do right ought to be cultivated into this habitual independence. In other words, this state of the will is a means to good, not intrinsically a good, and does not contradict the doctrine that nothing is a good to human beings except insofar as it is either itself pleasurable, or a means of attaining pleasure or averting pain.

4.10.oldText: But if this doctrine is true, the principle of utility is proved. Whether it is so or not must now be left to the consideration of the thoughtful reader.

5.0.oldText: In every age of speculation, one of the strongest obstacles to accepting the doctrine that Utility or Happiness is the criterion of right and wrong has come from the idea of Justice. The powerful sentiment, and apparently clear perception, that the word calls up with the speed and certainty of an instinct, has seemed to most thinkers to point to an inherent quality in things — to show that the Just must have an existence in Nature as something absolute, generically distinct from every variety of the Expedient, and conceptually opposed to it, even though (as is commonly granted) never, in the long run, actually separated from it in fact.

5.1.oldText: In this, as in our other moral sentiments, there is no necessary connection between the question of its origin and the question of its binding force. That a feeling is given to us by Nature does not necessarily legitimate all its promptings. The feeling of justice might be a peculiar instinct, and might still need, like our other instincts, to be controlled and enlightened by a higher reason. If we have intellectual instincts that lead us to judge in a particular way, just as we have animal instincts that prompt us to act in a particular way, there is no necessity that the former should be more infallible in their sphere than the latter in theirs. It may just as well happen that wrong judgments are occasionally suggested by the one as wrong actions by the other. But although it is one thing to believe that we have natural feelings of justice and another to acknowledge them as an ultimate criterion of conduct, these two opinions are very closely connected in practice. Mankind are always predisposed to believe that any subjective feeling not otherwise accounted for is a revelation of some objective reality. Our present object is to determine whether the reality to which the feeling of justice corresponds is one that needs any such special revelation; whether the justice or injustice of an action is something intrinsically peculiar and distinct from all its other qualities, or only a combination of certain of those qualities presented under a particular aspect. For the purpose of this inquiry it is practically important to consider whether the feeling itself, of justice and injustice, is sui generis like our sensations of colour and taste, or a derivative feeling formed by a combination of others. This is the more essential to examine because people are generally willing enough to admit that, objectively, the dictates of justice coincide with a part of the field of General Expediency. But because the subjective mental feeling of Justice is different from that which commonly attaches to mere expediency, and, except in extreme cases of the latter, is far more imperative in its demands, people find it difficult to see in Justice only a particular kind or branch of general utility, and think that its superior binding force requires a totally different origin.

5.2.oldText: To throw light on this question, we must try to ascertain what the distinguishing character of justice, or of injustice, is — what is the quality, or whether there is any quality, attributed in common to all modes of conduct designated as unjust (for justice, like many other moral attributes, is best defined by its opposite) and distinguishing them from those modes of conduct that are disapproved without having that particular term of disapproval applied to them. If, in everything that people are accustomed to call just or unjust, some one common attribute or set of attributes is always present, we may judge whether this attribute or combination of attributes is capable of gathering around it a sentiment of that peculiar character and intensity by virtue of the general laws of our emotional constitution, or whether the sentiment is inexplicable and has to be regarded as a special provision of Nature. If we find the former to be the case, in resolving this question we will have resolved the main problem too; if the latter, we shall have to seek some other mode of investigating it.

5.3.oldText: To find the common attributes of a variety of objects, we have to begin by surveying the objects themselves in the concrete. Let us therefore look in turn at the various modes of action, and arrangements of human affairs, which are classed by universal or widely held opinion as Just or as Unjust. The things well known to excite the sentiments associated with those names are of a very mixed character. I shall pass them rapidly in review without studying any particular arrangement.

5.4.oldText: First, it is generally considered unjust to deprive anyone of his personal liberty, his property, or any other thing that belongs to him by law. Here, then, is one instance of the application of the terms just and unjust in a perfectly definite sense, namely, that it is just to respect, and unjust to violate, the legal rights of anyone. But this judgment admits of several exceptions, arising from the other forms in which the notions of justice and injustice present themselves. For example, the person who suffers the deprivation may (as the phrase is) have forfeited the rights of which he is deprived — a case to which we shall return shortly. But also,

5.5.oldText: Secondly: the legal rights of which he is deprived may be rights which ought not to have belonged to him — in other words, the law that confers these rights on him may be a bad law. When it is, or when (which amounts to the same thing for our purpose) it is supposed to be, opinions will differ as to the justice or injustice of breaking it. Some hold that no law, however bad, ought to be disobeyed by an individual citizen; that his opposition to it, if shown at all, should only be shown by trying to get it altered by the competent authority. This opinion (which condemns many of the most illustrious benefactors of mankind, and would often protect harmful institutions against the only weapons that, in the state of things existing at the time, have any chance of succeeding against them) is defended by those who hold it on grounds of expediency, principally the importance, to the common interest of mankind, of maintaining inviolate the sentiment of submission to law. Others, on the contrary, hold the directly opposite opinion: that any law judged to be bad may blamelessly be disobeyed, even though it is not judged to be unjust but only inexpedient. Others would confine the licence of disobedience to the case of unjust laws. But again, some say that all laws which are inexpedient are unjust, since every law imposes some restriction on the natural liberty of mankind, and this restriction is an injustice unless legitimated by tending to their good. Among these diversities of opinion, it seems to be universally admitted that there may be unjust laws, and that law consequently is not the ultimate criterion of justice, but may give to one person a benefit, or impose on another an evil, which justice condemns. When a law is thought to be unjust, however, it always seems to be regarded as unjust in the same way a breach of law is unjust — namely, by infringing somebody's right. That right, since it cannot in this case be a legal right, receives a different name and is called a moral right. We may say, therefore, that a second case of injustice consists in taking or withholding from any person what he has a moral right to.

5.6.oldText: Thirdly, it is universally considered just that each person should obtain that (whether good or evil) which he deserves, and unjust that he should obtain a good, or be made to undergo an evil, which he does not deserve. This is perhaps the clearest and most emphatic form in which the idea of justice is conceived by the general mind. Since it involves the notion of desert, the question arises: what constitutes desert? Speaking generally, a person is understood to deserve good if he does right, evil if he does wrong; and in a more particular sense, to deserve good from those to whom he does, or has done, good, and evil from those to whom he does, or has done, evil. The precept of returning good for evil has never been regarded as a case of fulfilling justice, but as one in which the claims of justice are waived in obedience to other considerations.

5.7.oldText: Fourthly, it is admittedly unjust to break faith with anyone — to violate an engagement, either express or implied, or to disappoint expectations raised by our own conduct, at least if we have raised those expectations knowingly and voluntarily. Like the other obligations of justice already mentioned, this one is not regarded as absolute, but as capable of being overridden by a stronger obligation of justice on the other side, or by such conduct on the part of the person concerned as is considered to absolve us from our obligation to him, and to constitute a forfeiture of the benefit which he has been led to expect.

5.8.oldText: Fifthly, by universal admission, it is inconsistent with justice to be partial — to show favour or preference to one person over another in matters to which favour and preference do not properly apply. Impartiality, however, does not seem to be regarded as a duty in itself, but rather as instrumental to some other duty. It is admitted that favour and preference are not always blameworthy, and indeed the cases in which they are condemned are the exception rather than the rule. A person would be more likely to be blamed than applauded for giving his family or friends no preference in good offices over strangers when he could do so without violating any other duty, and no one thinks it unjust to seek one person rather than another as a friend, connection, or companion. Impartiality where rights are concerned is of course obligatory, but this is included in the more general obligation of giving everyone his right. A tribunal, for example, must be impartial because it is bound to award, without regard to any other consideration, a disputed object to the one of two parties who has the right to it. There are other cases in which impartiality means being solely influenced by desert, as with those who, in the role of judges, teachers, or parents, administer reward and punishment as such. There are cases, again, in which it means being solely influenced by regard for the public interest, as in making a selection among candidates for a government post. Impartiality, in short, as an obligation of justice, may be said to mean being exclusively influenced by the considerations which are supposed to influence the particular case in hand, and resisting the pull of any motives that prompt to conduct different from what those considerations would dictate.

5.9.oldText: Closely allied to the idea of impartiality is that of equality, which often enters as a component part both into the conception of justice and into the practice of it, and in the eyes of many people constitutes its essence. But in this, even more than in any other case, the notion of justice varies in different people, and always conforms in its variations to their notion of utility. Each person maintains that equality is the dictate of justice, except where he thinks expediency requires inequality. The justice of giving equal protection to the rights of all is upheld by those who support the most outrageous inequality in the rights themselves. Even in slave countries it is theoretically admitted that the rights of the slave, such as they are, ought to be as sacred as those of the master, and that a tribunal which fails to enforce them with equal strictness is wanting in justice; while at the same time institutions which leave the slave hardly any rights to enforce are not deemed unjust, because they are not deemed inexpedient. Those who think utility requires distinctions of rank do not consider it unjust that riches and social privileges should be unequally distributed; but those who think this inequality inexpedient think it unjust as well. Whoever thinks government is necessary sees no injustice in as much inequality as is constituted by giving the magistrate powers not granted to other people. Even among those who hold levelling doctrines, there are as many questions of justice as there are differences of opinion about expediency. Some Communists consider it unjust that the product of the labour of the community should be shared on any other principle than that of exact equality. Others think it just that those should receive most whose needs are greatest. Others hold that those who work harder, or who produce more, or whose services are more valuable to the community, may justly claim a larger share in the division of the product. And the sense of natural justice may be plausibly appealed to on behalf of every one of these opinions.

5.10.oldText: Among so many diverse applications of the term Justice, which is nonetheless not regarded as ambiguous, it is somewhat difficult to grasp the mental link that holds them together, and on which the moral sentiment attached to the term essentially depends. Perhaps, in this difficulty, some help may be drawn from the history of the word, as indicated by its etymology.

5.11.oldText: In most languages, if not in all, the etymology of the word that corresponds to Just points to an origin connected either with positive law or with what was in most cases the primitive form of law — authoritative custom. Justum is a form of jussum, that which has been ordered. Jus is of the same origin. Dikaion comes from dikē, whose principal meaning, at least in the historical ages of Greece, was a lawsuit. Originally it meant only the mode or manner of doing things, but it early came to mean the prescribed manner — that which the recognised authorities (patriarchal, judicial, or political) would enforce. Recht, from which came right and righteous, is synonymous with law. The original meaning of recht did not point to law but to physical straightness, just as wrong and its Latin equivalents meant twisted or crooked; from this it is argued that right did not originally mean law, but on the contrary, law meant right. However that may be, the fact that recht and droit became restricted in their meaning to positive law — even though much that is not required by law is equally necessary to moral straightness or rectitude — is just as telling about the original character of moral ideas as if the derivation had gone the other way. The courts of justice, the administration of justice, are the courts and the administration of law. La justice, in French, is the established term for the judiciary. There can, I think, be no doubt that the idée mère, the primitive element, in the formation of the notion of justice was conformity to law. It constituted the entire idea among the Hebrews up to the birth of Christianity, as one would expect with a people whose laws attempted to cover every subject on which precepts were required, and who believed those laws to be a direct emanation from the Supreme Being. But other nations, particularly the Greeks and Romans, who knew that their laws had been made originally, and still continued to be made, by people, were not afraid to admit that those people might make bad laws — might do, by law, the same things, and from the same motives, that, if done by individuals without the sanction of law, would be called unjust. Hence the sentiment of injustice came to be attached not to all violations of law, but only to violations of such laws as ought to exist (including those that ought to exist but do not), and to laws themselves, if supposed to be contrary to what ought to be law. In this way, the idea of law and of its commands was still predominant in the notion of justice, even when the laws actually in force ceased to be accepted as the standard of it.

5.12.oldText: It is true that mankind consider the idea of justice and its obligations as applicable to many things that neither are, nor is it desired that they should be, regulated by law. Nobody wants laws to interfere with the whole detail of private life, yet everyone allows that in all daily conduct a person may, and does, show himself to be either just or unjust. But even here, the idea of the breach of what ought to be law still lingers in a modified shape. It would always give us pleasure, and chime in with our feelings of fitness, that acts we deem unjust should be punished, though we do not always think it expedient that this should be done by the tribunals. We forgo that gratification because of incidental inconveniences. We should be glad to see just conduct enforced and injustice repressed, even in the minutest details, if we were not, with reason, afraid of trusting the magistrate with so unlimited a power over individuals. When we think a person is bound in justice to do something, it is an ordinary form of language to say that he ought to be compelled to do it. We should be gratified to see the obligation enforced by anybody who had the power. If we see that its enforcement by law would be inexpedient, we lament the impossibility, we regard the impunity given to injustice as an evil, and try to make amends for it by bringing a strong expression of our own and the public's disapproval to bear on the offender. Thus the idea of legal constraint is still the generating idea of the notion of justice, though it undergoes several transformations before that notion, as it exists in an advanced state of society, becomes complete.

5.13.oldText: The above is, I think, a true account, as far as it goes, of the origin and progressive growth of the idea of justice. But we must observe that it contains, as yet, nothing to distinguish that obligation from moral obligation in general. For the truth is that the idea of penal sanction, which is the essence of law, enters not only into the conception of injustice but into that of any kind of wrong. We do not call anything wrong unless we mean to imply that a person ought to be punished in some way for doing it — if not by law, then by the opinion of his fellow creatures; if not by opinion, then by the reproaches of his own conscience. This seems the real turning point of the distinction between morality and mere expediency. It is part of the notion of Duty in every one of its forms that a person may rightfully be compelled to fulfil it. Duty is something that may be exacted from a person as one exacts a debt. Unless we think it might be exacted from him, we do not call it his duty. Reasons of prudence, or the interests of other people, may weigh against actually exacting it, but the person himself, it is clearly understood, would not be entitled to complain. There are other things, on the contrary, that we wish people would do, that we like or admire them for doing, perhaps dislike or despise them for not doing, but yet admit they are not bound to do; it is not a case of moral obligation. We do not blame them — that is, we do not think they are proper objects of punishment. How we come by these ideas of deserving and not deserving punishment will appear, perhaps, later; but I think there is no doubt that this distinction lies at the bottom of the notions of right and wrong: we call any conduct wrong, or use instead some other term of dislike or disparagement, according to whether we think the person ought, or ought not, to be punished for it. We say it would be right to do such-and-such, or merely that it would be desirable or laudable, depending on whether we would wish to see the person concerned compelled, or only persuaded and exhorted, to act in that manner.[C]

5.14.oldText: This, then, being the characteristic difference that marks off — not justice, but morality in general — from the remaining provinces of Expediency and Worthiness, the character is still to be sought which distinguishes justice from the other branches of morality. Now it is known that ethical writers divide moral duties into two classes, denoted by the ill-chosen expressions, duties of perfect and of imperfect obligation. The latter are those in which, though the act is obligatory, the particular occasions for performing it are left to our choice — as in the case of charity or beneficence, which we are bound to practise but not towards any definite person, nor at any prescribed time. In the more precise language of philosophical jurists, duties of perfect obligation are those duties in virtue of which a correlative right resides in some person or persons; duties of imperfect obligation are those moral obligations which give birth to no right. I think it will be found that this distinction exactly coincides with the one between justice and the other obligations of morality. In our survey of the various popular meanings of justice, the term appeared generally to involve the idea of a personal right — a claim on the part of one or more individuals, like that which the law gives when it confers a proprietary or other legal right. Whether the injustice consists in depriving a person of a possession, in breaking faith with him, in treating him worse than he deserves, or worse than other people who have no greater claims, in each case the supposition implies two things: a wrong done, and some assignable person who is wronged. Injustice may also be done by treating a person better than others; but the wrong in this case is to his competitors, who are also assignable people. It seems to me that this feature in the case — a right in some person, correlative to the moral obligation — constitutes the specific difference between justice, and generosity or beneficence. Justice implies something that it is not only right to do, and wrong not to do, but that some individual person can claim from us as his moral right. No one has a moral right to our generosity or beneficence, because we are not morally bound to practise those virtues towards any given individual. And it will be found, with regard to this as with every correct definition, that the instances which seem to conflict with it are those which most confirm it. For if a moralist tries, as some have done, to argue that mankind generally — though not any given individual — has a right to all the good we can do them, he at once, by that thesis, includes generosity and beneficence within the category of justice. He is obliged to say that our utmost exertions are due to our fellow creatures, thereby treating them as a debt; or that nothing less can be a sufficient return for what society does for us, thereby classing the case as one of gratitude. Both are acknowledged cases of justice. Wherever there is a right, the case is one of justice, and not of the virtue of beneficence; and whoever does not place the distinction between justice and morality in general where we have now placed it will be found to make no distinction between them at all, but to merge all morality in justice.

5.15.oldText: Having thus tried to determine the distinctive elements that enter into the composition of the idea of justice, we are ready to take up the inquiry whether the feeling that accompanies the idea is attached to it by a special dispensation of nature, or whether it could have grown up, by any known laws, out of the idea itself — and in particular, whether it can have originated in considerations of general expediency.

5.16.oldText: I take it that the sentiment itself does not arise from anything that would commonly, or correctly, be called an idea of expediency — but that, though the sentiment does not, whatever is moral in it does.

5.17.oldText: We have seen that the two essential ingredients in the sentiment of justice are the desire to punish a person who has done harm, and the knowledge or belief that there is some definite individual or individuals to whom harm has been done.

5.18.oldText: Now it appears to me that the desire to punish a person who has done harm to some individual is a spontaneous outgrowth from two sentiments, both in the highest degree natural, and either of which is, or resembles, an instinct: the impulse of self-defence and the feeling of sympathy.

5.19.oldText: It is natural to resent, and to repel or retaliate, any harm done or attempted against ourselves, or against those with whom we sympathise. The origin of this sentiment need not be discussed here. Whether it is an instinct or a result of intelligence, we know that it is common to all animal nature; for every animal tries to hurt those who have hurt, or who it thinks are about to hurt, itself or its young. Human beings, on this point, only differ from other animals in two respects. First, in being capable of sympathising not only with their offspring, or, like some of the nobler animals, with some superior animal who is kind to them, but with all human, and even with all sentient, beings. Secondly, in having a more developed intelligence, which gives a wider range to the whole of their sentiments, whether self-regarding or sympathetic. By virtue of his superior intelligence, even apart from his wider range of sympathy, a human being is capable of grasping a community of interest between himself and the human society of which he forms a part, such that any conduct which threatens the security of society generally is threatening to his own, and calls forth his instinct (if instinct it is) of self-defence. The same superiority of intelligence, joined to the power of sympathising with human beings generally, enables him to attach himself to the collective idea of his tribe, his country, or mankind, in such a way that any act hurtful to them rouses his instinct of sympathy and prompts him to resistance.

5.20.oldText: The sentiment of justice, in that one of its elements which consists of the desire to punish, is therefore, I take it, the natural feeling of retaliation or vengeance, made by intellect and sympathy applicable to those injuries — those hurts which wound us through, or in common with, society at large. This sentiment, in itself, has nothing moral in it. What is moral is the exclusive subordination of it to the social sympathies, so as to wait on and obey their call. For the natural feeling tends to make us resent indiscriminately whatever anyone does that is disagreeable to us; but when moralised by the social feeling, it acts only in directions conformable to the general good. Just people resent a hurt to society though it is not otherwise a hurt to themselves, and do not resent a hurt to themselves, however painful, unless it is of the kind which society has a common interest with them in repressing.

5.21.oldText: It is no objection to this doctrine to say that when we feel our sense of justice outraged, we are not thinking of society at large, or of any collective interest, but only of the individual case. It is common enough, though the reverse of commendable, to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain. But a person whose resentment is really a moral feeling — that is, who considers whether an act is blameable before he allows himself to resent it — such a person, though he may not say to himself in so many words that he is standing up for the interest of society, certainly does feel that he is asserting a rule which is for the benefit of others as well as for his own. If he is not feeling this — if he is regarding the act solely as it affects him individually — he is not consciously just; he is not concerning himself about the justice of his actions. This is admitted even by anti-utilitarian moralists. When Kant (as already noted) propounds as the fundamental principle of morals, 'Act so that your rule of conduct might be adopted as a law by all rational beings,' he virtually acknowledges that the interest of mankind collectively, or at least of mankind indiscriminately, must be in the agent's mind when conscientiously deciding on the morality of the act. Otherwise he uses words without meaning; for it cannot even plausibly be maintained that a rule of utter selfishness could not possibly be adopted by all rational beings, or that there is any insuperable obstacle in the nature of things to its being adopted. To give Kant's principle any meaning, the sense put on it must be that we ought to shape our conduct by a rule which all rational beings might adopt with benefit to their collective interest.

5.22.oldText: To recap: the idea of justice supposes two things — a rule of conduct, and a sentiment that sanctions the rule. The first must be supposed common to all mankind and intended for their good. The other (the sentiment) is a desire that punishment may be suffered by those who break the rule. There is also involved the conception of some definite person who suffers by the breach, whose rights (to use the language appropriate to the case) are violated by it. And the sentiment of justice appears to me to be the animal desire to repel or retaliate a hurt or damage to oneself, or to those with whom one sympathises, widened to include all people through the human capacity of enlarged sympathy and the human conception of intelligent self-interest. From the latter elements the feeling gets its morality; from the former, its peculiar impressiveness and energy of self-assertion.

5.23.oldText: Throughout, I have treated the idea of a right residing in the injured person, and violated by the injury, not as a separate element in the composition of the idea and sentiment, but as one of the forms in which the other two elements clothe themselves. Those elements are: a hurt to some assignable person or persons on the one hand, and a demand for punishment on the other. An examination of our own minds, I think, will show that these two things include everything we mean when we speak of violation of a right. When we call anything a person's right, we mean that he has a valid claim on society to protect him in the possession of it, either by the force of law or by that of education and opinion. If he has what we consider a sufficient claim, on whatever ground, to have something guaranteed to him by society, we say that he has a right to it. If we want to prove that something does not belong to him by right, we think this proved as soon as it is admitted that society ought not to take measures to secure it for him, but should leave it to chance, or to his own exertions. Thus a person is said to have a right to what he can earn in fair professional competition, because society ought not to allow any other person to hinder him from trying to earn in that way as much as he can. But he has no right to three hundred pounds a year, though he may happen to be earning it, because society is not called on to provide that he shall earn that sum. On the contrary, if he owns ten thousand pounds of three-per-cent stock, he does have a right to three hundred a year, because society has come under an obligation to provide him with an income of that amount.

5.24.oldText: To have a right, then, is, I take it, to have something which society ought to defend me in the possession of. If the objector goes on to ask why society ought to, I can give him no other reason than general utility. If that expression does not seem to convey a sufficient sense of the strength of the obligation, or to account for the peculiar energy of the feeling, it is because there enters into the composition of the sentiment not only a rational but also an animal element — the thirst for retaliation. This thirst derives its intensity, as well as its moral justification, from the extraordinarily important and impressive kind of utility involved. The interest at stake is that of security, the most vital of all interests to everyone's feelings. Nearly all other earthly benefits are needed by one person and not by another, and many of them can, if necessary, be cheerfully forgone or replaced by something else. But security no human being can possibly do without. On it we depend for all our immunity from evil, and for the whole value of all and every good, beyond the passing moment; since nothing but the gratification of the instant would be of any worth to us if we could be deprived of everything the next instant by whoever happened to be momentarily stronger than ourselves. Now this most indispensable of all necessaries, after physical nutriment, cannot be had unless the machinery for providing it is kept ceaselessly in active play. Our notion, therefore, of the claim we have on our fellow creatures to join in making safe for us the very groundwork of our existence gathers feelings around it so much more intense than those involved in any of the more common cases of utility, that the difference in degree (as is often the case in psychology) becomes a real difference in kind. The claim takes on that character of absoluteness, that apparent infinity, and incommensurability with all other considerations, which constitute the distinction between the feeling of right and wrong and that of ordinary expediency and inexpediency. The feelings involved are so powerful, and we count so positively on finding a corresponding feeling in others (all being alike interested), that ought and should grow into must, and recognised indispensability becomes a moral necessity, analogous to physical necessity, and often not inferior to it in binding force.

5.25.oldText: If the preceding analysis, or something like it, is not the correct account of the notion of justice; if justice is totally independent of utility, and is a standard per se which the mind can recognise by simple introspection — it is hard to understand why that internal oracle is so ambiguous, and why so many things appear either just or unjust according to the light in which they are regarded. We are continually told that Utility is an uncertain standard, which every different person interprets differently, and that there is no safety except in the immutable, ineffaceable, and unmistakable dictates of Justice, which carry their evidence in themselves and are independent of the fluctuations of opinion. One would suppose from this that on questions of justice there could be no controversy; that if we take justice as our rule, its application to any given case could leave us in as little doubt as a mathematical demonstration. So far is this from being the case that there is as much difference of opinion, and as fierce dispute, about what is just as about what is useful to society. Not only do different nations and individuals have different notions of justice; even in the mind of one and the same person, justice is not some single rule, principle, or maxim, but many — which do not always coincide in their dictates, and in choosing between which he is guided either by some external standard or by his own personal preferences.

5.26.oldText: For instance, there are some who say it is unjust to punish anyone for the sake of example to others, that punishment is just only when intended for the good of the sufferer himself. Others maintain the extreme reverse, contending that to punish people who have reached years of discretion for their own benefit is despotism and injustice — since, if the matter at issue is solely their own good, no one has a right to override their own judgment of it; but they may justly be punished to prevent harm to others, this being an exercise of the legitimate right of self-defence. Mr. Owen, again, affirms that it is unjust to punish at all, because the criminal did not make his own character; his education and the circumstances surrounding him have made him a criminal, and for these he is not responsible. All these opinions are extremely plausible, and so long as the question is argued solely as one of justice, without going down to the principles which underlie justice and are the source of its authority, I do not see how any of these reasoners can be refuted. For in truth every one of the three builds on rules of justice that are admittedly true. The first appeals to the acknowledged injustice of singling out an individual and making him a sacrifice, without his consent, for other people's benefit. The second relies on the acknowledged justice of self-defence and the admitted injustice of forcing one person to conform to another's notion of what constitutes his good. The Owenite invokes the admitted principle that it is unjust to punish anyone for what he cannot help. Each is triumphant so long as he is not compelled to take into consideration any other maxims of justice than the one he has chosen; but as soon as their several maxims are brought face to face, each disputant seems to have exactly as much to say for himself as the others. None of them can carry out his own notion of justice without trampling on another equally binding. These are difficulties; they have always been felt to be so, and many devices have been invented to evade rather than overcome them. As a refuge from the last of the three, people imagined what they called the freedom of the will, fancying that they could not justify punishing a man whose will was in a thoroughly hateful state unless it could be supposed to have come into that state through no influence of prior circumstances. To escape from the other difficulties, a favourite contrivance has been the fiction of a contract, by which at some unknown period all the members of society engaged to obey the laws, and consented to be punished for any disobedience to them, thereby giving their legislators the right (which it is assumed they would not otherwise have had) to punish them, either for their own good or for that of society. This happy thought was considered to dispose of the whole difficulty and to legitimate the infliction of punishment, by virtue of another received maxim of justice, volenti non fit injuria — that is not unjust which is done with the consent of the person who is supposed to be hurt by it. I need hardly remark that even if the consent were not a mere fiction, this maxim is not superior in authority to the others which it is brought in to supersede. It is, on the contrary, an instructive specimen of the loose and irregular way in which supposed principles of justice grow up. This particular one evidently came into use as an aid to the rough necessities of courts of law, which are sometimes obliged to be content with very uncertain presumptions because of the greater evils that would often arise from any attempt on their part to cut finer. But even courts of law are not able to adhere consistently to the maxim, since they allow voluntary engagements to be set aside on the grounds of fraud, and sometimes of mere mistake or misinformation.

5.27.oldText: Again, once the legitimacy of inflicting punishment is admitted, how many conflicting conceptions of justice come to light in discussing the proper apportionment of punishment to offences. No rule on this subject recommends itself so strongly to the primitive and spontaneous sentiment of justice as the lex talionis — an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Though this principle of Jewish and of Muslim law has generally been abandoned in Europe as a practical maxim, there is, I suspect, in most minds, a secret hankering after it; and when retribution accidentally falls on an offender in that precise shape, the general feeling of satisfaction shown bears witness to how natural is the sentiment which finds this repayment in kind acceptable. For many, the test of justice in inflicting punishment is that the punishment should be proportioned to the offence — meaning that it should be exactly measured by the moral guilt of the culprit (whatever their standard for measuring moral guilt). The question how much punishment is needed to deter from the offence has nothing to do with the question of justice, in their estimation. There are others, by contrast, for whom that consideration is all in all; who maintain that it is not just, at least for man, to inflict on a fellow creature, whatever his offences may be, any amount of suffering beyond the least that will suffice to prevent him from repeating, and others from imitating, his misconduct.

5.28.oldText: To take another example from a subject already referred to once: in a cooperative industrial association, is it just or not that talent or skill should give a claim to higher pay? On the negative side it is argued that whoever does the best he can deserves equally well, and ought not in justice to be placed in a position of inferiority through no fault of his own; that superior abilities have more than enough advantages already, in the admiration they excite, the personal influence they command, and the internal sources of satisfaction attending them, without adding to these a larger share of the world's goods; and that society is bound in justice to make compensation to the less favoured for this unmerited inequality of advantages, rather than to make it worse. On the other side, it is contended that society receives more from the more efficient labourer; that since his services are more useful, society owes him a larger return for them; that a greater share of the joint result is actually his work, and that not to allow his claim to it is a kind of robbery; that if he is to receive only as much as others, he can only justly be required to produce as much, and to give a smaller amount of time and exertion, proportioned to his greater efficiency. Who is to decide between these appeals to conflicting principles of justice? Justice in this case has two sides which it is impossible to bring into harmony, and the two disputants have chosen opposite sides — one looks to what it is just that the individual should receive, the other to what it is just that the community should give. Each, from his own point of view, is unanswerable, and any choice between them on grounds of justice must be perfectly arbitrary. Social utility alone can decide the preference.

5.29.oldText: How many, again, and how irreconcilable, are the standards of justice referred to in discussing the apportionment of taxation. One opinion is that payment to the State should be in numerical proportion to financial means. Others think that justice dictates what they call graduated taxation — taking a higher percentage from those who have more to spare. As a matter of natural justice, a strong case might be made for disregarding means altogether and taking the same absolute sum (whenever it could be got) from everyone — just as the subscribers to a mess, or to a club, all pay the same sum for the same privileges, whether they can all equally afford it or not. Since (it might be said) the protection of law and government is given to, and is equally required by, all, there is no injustice in making all buy it at the same price. It is reckoned justice, not injustice, that a dealer should charge all customers the same price for the same article, not a price varying with their means of payment. This doctrine, as applied to taxation, finds no advocates, because it conflicts strongly with people's feelings of humanity and perceptions of social expediency; but the principle of justice it invokes is as true and as binding as those which can be appealed to against it. Accordingly, it exerts a tacit influence on the line of defence used for other modes of assessing taxation. People feel obliged to argue that the State does more for the rich than for the poor, as a justification for its taking more from them — though this is in reality not true, for the rich would be far better able to protect themselves in the absence of law or government than the poor, and indeed would probably be successful in converting the poor into their slaves. Others, again, so far defer to the same conception of justice as to maintain that all should pay an equal capitation tax for the protection of their persons (these being of equal value to all), and an unequal tax for the protection of their property, which is unequal. To this others reply that the all of one man is as valuable to him as the all of another. From these confusions there is no mode of extrication other than the utilitarian.

5.30.oldText: Is, then, the difference between the Just and the Expedient a merely imaginary distinction? Have mankind been under a delusion in thinking that justice is a more sacred thing than policy, and that the latter ought only to be listened to after the former has been satisfied? By no means. The account we have given of the nature and origin of the sentiment recognises a real distinction; and no one of those who profess the most sublime contempt for the consequences of actions as an element in their morality attaches more importance to the distinction than I do. While I dispute the pretensions of any theory that sets up an imaginary standard of justice not grounded on utility, I account the justice grounded on utility to be the chief part, and incomparably the most sacred and binding part, of all morality. Justice is a name for certain classes of moral rules which concern the essentials of human well-being more nearly, and are therefore of more absolute obligation, than any other rules for the guidance of life; and the notion we have found to be of the essence of the idea of justice — that of a right residing in an individual — implies and testifies to this more binding obligation.

5.31.oldText: The moral rules which forbid mankind to hurt one another (in which we must never forget to include wrongful interference with each other's freedom) are more vital to human well-being than any maxims, however important, which only point out the best way of managing some department of human affairs. They also have this peculiarity, that they are the main element in determining the whole of the social feelings of mankind. Their observance alone preserves peace between human beings; if obedience to them were not the rule and disobedience the exception, everyone would see in everyone else a probable enemy against whom he must be perpetually on guard. What is hardly less important, these are the precepts which people have the strongest and most direct inducements to impress on one another. By merely giving each other prudential advice or exhortation, they may gain, or think they gain, nothing; in inculcating on each other the duty of positive beneficence they have an unmistakable interest, but far less in degree — a person may possibly not need the benefits of others, but he always needs that they should not do him harm. Thus the moralities which protect every individual from being harmed by others, either directly or by being hindered in his freedom to pursue his own good, are at once those which he himself has most at heart and those which he has the strongest interest in publishing and enforcing by word and deed. It is by a person's observance of these that his fitness to exist as one of the fellowship of human beings is tested and decided; for on that depends whether he is a nuisance or not to those with whom he is in contact. Now it is these moralities primarily that compose the obligations of justice. The most marked cases of injustice, and those which give the tone to the feeling of repugnance characterising the sentiment, are acts of wrongful aggression, or wrongful exercise of power over someone; the next are those that consist in wrongfully withholding from him something which is his due. In both cases, a positive hurt is inflicted on him, either in the form of direct suffering, or of the privation of some good which he had reasonable ground — either of a physical or a social kind — for counting on.

5.32.oldText: The same powerful motives that command the observance of these primary moralities enjoin the punishment of those who violate them. As the impulses of self-defence, of defence of others, and of vengeance are all called forth against such people, retribution, or evil for evil, becomes closely connected with the sentiment of justice and is universally included in the idea. Good for good is also one of the dictates of justice, and this, though its social utility is evident and though it carries with it a natural human feeling, does not at first sight have the obvious connection with hurt or injury which, present in the most elementary cases of just and unjust, is the source of the characteristic intensity of the sentiment. But the connection, though less obvious, is no less real. He who accepts benefits and denies a return of them when needed inflicts a real hurt by disappointing one of the most natural and reasonable of expectations, and one which he must at least tacitly have encouraged, otherwise the benefits would seldom have been given. The important rank, among human evils and wrongs, of the disappointment of expectation is shown in the fact that it constitutes the principal criminality of two such highly immoral acts as a breach of friendship and a breach of promise. Few hurts that human beings can suffer are greater, and none wound more, than when what they habitually and with full assurance relied on fails them in the hour of need; and few wrongs are greater than this mere withholding of good. None excite more resentment, either in the person suffering or in a sympathising spectator. The principle, therefore, of giving each what they deserve — that is, good for good as well as evil for evil — is not only included within the idea of Justice as we have defined it, but is a proper object of that intensity of sentiment which places the Just, in human estimation, above the simply Expedient.

5.33.oldText: Most of the maxims of justice current in the world, and commonly appealed to in its transactions, are simply instrumental to carrying into effect the principles of justice we have just spoken of. That a person is only responsible for what he has done voluntarily, or could voluntarily have avoided; that it is unjust to condemn anyone unheard; that the punishment ought to be proportioned to the offence — and the like — are maxims intended to prevent the just principle of evil for evil from being perverted into the infliction of evil without that justification. Most of these common maxims have come into use from the practice of courts of justice, which have naturally been led to a more complete recognition and elaboration than was likely to suggest itself to others, of the rules necessary to enable them to fulfil their double function of inflicting punishment when due, and of awarding to each person his right.

5.34.oldText: That first of judicial virtues, impartiality, is an obligation of justice partly for the reason just mentioned — as being a necessary condition of fulfilling the other obligations of justice. But this is not the only source of the exalted rank, among human obligations, of those maxims of equality and impartiality which, both in popular estimation and in that of the most enlightened, are included among the precepts of justice. From one point of view, they may be considered corollaries of the principles already laid down. If it is a duty to do to each according to his deserts — returning good for good as well as repressing evil by evil — it necessarily follows that we should treat all equally well (when no higher duty forbids) who have deserved equally well of us, and that society should treat all equally well who have deserved equally well of it — that is, who have deserved equally well absolutely. This is the highest abstract standard of social and distributive justice, towards which all institutions, and the efforts of all virtuous citizens, should be made to converge to the utmost possible degree. But this great moral duty rests on a still deeper foundation, being a direct emanation from the first principle of morals, and not a mere logical corollary of secondary or derivative doctrines. It is involved in the very meaning of Utility, or the Greatest-Happiness Principle. That principle is a mere form of words without rational meaning, unless one person's happiness, supposed equal in degree (with the proper allowance made for kind), is counted for exactly as much as another's. Those conditions being supplied, Bentham's dictum, 'everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one,' might be written under the principle of utility as an explanatory commentary.[D] The equal claim of everybody to happiness in the estimation of the moralist and the legislator involves an equal claim to all the means of happiness, except insofar as the inevitable conditions of human life and the general interest, in which that of every individual is included, set limits to the maxim — and those limits ought to be strictly construed. Like every other maxim of justice, this one is by no means applied or held applicable universally; on the contrary, as I have already remarked, it bends to every person's ideas of social expediency. But in whatever case it is deemed applicable at all, it is held to be a dictate of justice. All persons are deemed to have a right to equality of treatment, except when some recognised social expediency requires the reverse. Hence all social inequalities which have ceased to be considered expedient take on the character not of mere inexpediency but of injustice, and appear so tyrannical that people are apt to wonder how they ever could have been tolerated — forgetting that they themselves perhaps tolerate other inequalities under an equally mistaken notion of expediency, the correction of which would make what they approve seem just as monstrous as what they have at last learnt to condemn. The whole history of social improvement has been a series of transitions by which one custom or institution after another, from being a supposed primary necessity of social existence, has passed into the rank of a universally stigmatised injustice and tyranny. So it has been with the distinctions of slaves and freemen, nobles and serfs, patricians and plebeians; and so it will be, and in part already is, with the aristocracies of colour, race, and sex.

5.35.oldText: It appears from what has been said that justice is a name for certain moral requirements which, regarded collectively, stand higher in the scale of social utility, and are therefore of more paramount obligation, than any others — though particular cases may arise in which some other social duty is so important as to override any one of the general maxims of justice. Thus, to save a life, it may not only be allowable but a duty to steal, or take by force, the necessary food or medicine, or to kidnap and compel to officiate the only qualified medical practitioner. In such cases, since we do not call anything justice which is not a virtue, we usually say not that justice must give way to some other moral principle, but that what is just in ordinary cases is, by reason of that other principle, not just in the particular case. By this useful accommodation of language, the character of indefeasibility attributed to justice is kept up, and we are spared the necessity of maintaining that there can be laudable injustice.

5.36.oldText: The considerations now adduced resolve, I take it, the only real difficulty in the utilitarian theory of morals. It has always been evident that all cases of justice are also cases of expediency — the difference lies in the peculiar sentiment that attaches to the former, as contrasted with the latter. If this characteristic sentiment has been sufficiently accounted for; if there is no need to assume any peculiarity of origin for it; if it is simply the natural feeling of resentment, moralised by being made coextensive with the demands of social good; and if this feeling not only does but ought to exist in all the classes of cases to which the idea of justice corresponds — then that idea no longer presents itself as a stumbling block to utilitarian ethics. Justice remains the appropriate name for certain social utilities which are vastly more important, and therefore more absolute and imperative, than any others are as a class (though not more so than others may be in particular cases). It is therefore right that they should be, as they naturally are, guarded by a sentiment that differs not only in degree but also in kind from the milder feeling attaching to the mere idea of promoting human pleasure or convenience — distinguished by the more definite nature of its commands and by the sterner character of its sanctions.

5.37.oldText: [Footnote C: See this point enforced and illustrated by Professor Bain, in an admirable chapter (entitled "The Ethical Emotions, or the Moral Sense") of the second of the two treatises composing his elaborate and profound work on the Mind.]

5.38.oldText: [Footnote D: This implication, in the first principle of the utilitarian scheme, of perfect impartiality between persons, is regarded by Mr. Herbert Spencer (in his Social Statics) as a disproof of the claims of utility to be a sufficient guide to right, since (he says) the principle of utility presupposes the prior principle that everybody has an equal right to happiness. It may be more correctly described as supposing that equal amounts of happiness are equally desirable, whether felt by the same or by different persons. This, however, is not a presupposition — not a premise needed to support the principle of utility, but the very principle itself; for what is the principle of utility, if it is not that 'happiness' and 'desirable' are synonymous terms? If any prior principle is implied, it can be no other than this: that the truths of arithmetic are applicable to the valuation of happiness, as of all other measurable quantities. [Mr. Herbert Spencer, in a private communication on the subject of the preceding Note, objects to being considered an opponent of Utilitarianism, and states that he regards happiness as the ultimate end of morality, but deems that end only partially attainable by empirical generalisations from the observed results of conduct, and completely attainable only by deducing, from the laws of life and the conditions of existence, what kinds of action necessarily tend to produce happiness, and what kinds to produce unhappiness. With the exception of the word "necessarily," I have no dissent to express from this doctrine; and (omitting that word) I am not aware that any modern advocate of utilitarianism is of a different opinion. Bentham, certainly, to whom in the Social Statics Mr. Spencer particularly referred, is, least of all writers, chargeable with unwillingness to deduce the effect of actions on happiness from the laws of human nature and the universal conditions of human life. The common charge against him is of relying too exclusively on such deductions, and declining altogether to be bound by the generalisations from specific experience which Mr. Spencer thinks utilitarians generally confine themselves to. My own opinion (and, as I gather, Mr. Spencer's) is that in ethics, as in all other branches of scientific study, the consilience of the results of both these processes, each corroborating and verifying the other, is requisite to give to any general proposition the kind and degree of evidence which constitutes scientific proof.]]

1.0.oldText: Få træk ved vores nuværende viden er mere overraskende, eller mere afslørende for hvor lidt fremskridt vi har gjort i tænkningen om de vigtigste emner, end manglen på en afklaring i den lange debat om kriteriet for ret og uret. Fra filosofiens begyndelse er spørgsmålet om det højeste gode — som er det samme som at spørge, hvad moralen er grundet i — blevet behandlet som det centrale problem i den spekulative tænkning. Det har optaget de mest begavede sind og delt dem i rivaliserende skoler, der har ført en bitter intellektuel krig mod hinanden. Efter mere end to tusinde år fortsætter de samme stridigheder. Filosoffer stiller sig stadig op under de samme modstillede faner, og hverken professionelle tænkere eller menneskeheden som helhed synes at være kommet nærmere enighed end dengang den unge Sokrates lyttede til den gamle Protagoras og forsvarede (hvis Platons dialog hviler på en virkelig samtale) utilitarismens teori mod den såkaldte sofists folkelige moral.

1.1.oldText: Det er rigtigt, at en lignende forvirring og usikkerhed — og undertiden direkte uenighed — findes om førsteprincipperne i enhver videnskab, herunder den, der almindeligvis anses for den sikreste: matematikken. Alligevel skader det sjældent, og som regel slet ikke, troværdigheden af de konklusioner, disse videnskaber når frem til. Det tilsyneladende paradoks forklares ved, at en videnskabs detaljerede læresætninger sædvanligvis ikke udledes af, eller hviler på, det vi kalder dens førsteprincipper. Var det tilfældet, ville ingen videnskab stå svagere end algebraen, hvis sikkerhed ikke kommer fra de elementære aksiomer, som typisk bliver lært til begyndere — aksiomer som, sådan som nogle af dens mest fremtrædende lærere har formuleret dem, er lige så fulde af fiktioner som engelsk ret og lige så fulde af mysterier som teologi. De sandheder, som en videnskab i sidste ende accepterer som sine førsteprincipper, er i virkeligheden de endelige resultater af en metafysisk analyse anvendt på de grundbegreber, videnskaben arbejder med. Deres forhold til videnskaben er ikke som fundament til bygning, men som rødder til træ, der kan udføre deres opgave fuldstændigt godt, selv om de aldrig graves frem og kommer til syne. Men mens enkeltsandheder i videnskaberne kommer før den generelle teori, kunne man forvente det modsatte i en praktisk kunst som moral eller lovgivning. Enhver handling foretages for et formål, og handlingsregler synes at måtte tage hele deres karakter og tone fra det formål, de tjener. Når vi går i gang med et foretagende, ville en klar og præcis forestilling om, hvad vi forfølger, synes at være det første, vi har brug for — ikke det sidste, vi arbejder hen imod. En prøve på ret og uret må, skulle man tro, være midlet til at finde ud af, hvad der er ret eller uret, ikke en følge af, at man allerede har fundet ud af det.

1.2.oldText: Denne vanskelighed kan ikke omgås ved at appellere til den populære teori om en naturlig evne — en moralsk sans eller instinkt, der fortæller os, hvad der er ret og uret. For det første er selve eksistensen af et sådant moralsk instinkt en del af stridens emne. Og de tilhængere af det, der har nogen som helst pretention på filosofisk alvor, har været tvunget til at opgive idéen om, at det identificerer, hvad der er ret eller uret i et bestemt tilfælde, sådan som vores andre sanser identificerer et syn eller en lyd lige foran os. Vores moralske evne, ifølge alle dens fortolkere, der fortjener at blive kaldt tænkere, leverer os kun moralens almene principper. Den er en gren af fornuften, ikke af sansningen, og vi må søge i den efter moralens abstrakte læresætninger, ikke efter direkte sansning af moral i konkrete tilfælde. Den intuitive etiske skole insisterer, lige så meget som den såkaldte induktive skole, på nødvendigheden af almene love. Begge er enige om, at spørgsmålet om, hvorvidt en enkelt handling er moralsk, ikke er et spørgsmål om direkte sansning, men om at anvende en lov på et bestemt tilfælde. De anerkender også i vidt omfang de samme moralske love — men de er uenige om belægget for disse love og om kilden til deres autoritet. Ifølge den ene opfattelse er moralens principper selvindlysende a priori og kræver intet andet end at termernes betydning forstås. Ifølge den anden er ret og uret, ligesom sandt og falsk, spørgsmål om iagttagelse og erfaring. Men begge fastholder lige bestemt, at moralen må udledes af principper, og den intuitive skole hævder lige så stærkt som den induktive, at der findes en moralvidenskab. Alligevel forsøger de sjældent at opstille listen over de a priori-principper, som skulle tjene som denne videnskabs præmisser, og endnu sjældnere gør de noget forsøg på at føre disse forskellige principper tilbage til ét førsteprincip eller én fælles forpligtelsesgrund.
